title: Solve a linear equation without losing a term

section.heading: Solve a linear equation without losing a term
body: Undo additions before dividing by the coefficient of the variable. Distribute to every term inside parentheses. If fractions occur, multiply every term on both sides by a common denominator first; a minus sign outside parentheses changes every sign inside. Finish by substituting into the original equation.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(5 \left(x-2\right)=3 x+14\), distribute to get \(5 x-10=3 x+14\). Subtract 3 x and add \(10:2 x=24\), so \(x=12\). Check: both sides equal 50. With \(\frac{x+2}{3}-\frac{x-1}{6}=4\), multiply every term by \(6:2 \left(x+2\right)-\left(x-1\right)=24\), giving \(x=19\).

activity.prompt: What value of x satisfies \(4 \left(x-3\right)=2 x+8\)?
activity.explanation: Distribute: \(4 x-12=2 x+8\). Thus \(2 x=20\) and \(x=10\). The option 4 subtracts 12 in the wrong direction; 14 can result from undoing the parentheses incorrectly. Substitution gives 28 on both sides.

title: Eliminate a variable and interpret a system

section.heading: Eliminate a variable and interpret a system
body: Keep each equation true while adding multiples of equations to eliminate one variable. Substitute back to recover the other variable, then answer the requested sum or product. A third known variable is substituted first. If one equation is a multiple of the other, matching constants mean infinitely many solutions; inconsistent constants mean none.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(2 x+y=13\) and \(x-y=2\), add to get \(3 x=15\), so \(x=5\) and \(y=3\). If asked for xy, answer 15. In \(2 a+b=7\) and \(4 a+2 b=14\), the second equation repeats the first: every point on that line works. Replacing 14 by 15 would instead produce a contradiction.

activity.prompt: For \(x+y=11\) and \(2 x-y=7\), what is x−y?
activity.explanation: Adding gives \(3 x=18\), so \(x=6\). Then \(y=5\) and \(x-y=1\). The other choices are the individual variables, which are not the requested difference.

title: Split absolute-value equations and distance inequalities

section.heading: Split absolute-value equations and distance inequalities
body: Absolute value is distance, so \(\lvert u\rvert =a\) with \(a>0\) means \(u=a\) or \(u=-a\). Equal absolute values \(\lvert u\rvert =\lvert v\rvert\) mean \(u=v\) or \(u=-v\). For \(a>0\), \(\lvert u\rvert <a\) means \(-a<u<a\), while \(\lvert u\rvert >a\) means \(u<-a\) or \(u>a\). Preserve inclusive endpoints for \(\le\) or \(\ge\); a negative absolute-value target has no solution.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\lvert 3 x+2\rvert =10\), solve \(3 x+2=10\) and \(3 x+2=-10\), giving \(x=\frac{8}{3}\) and \(x=-4\). For \(\lvert x+1\rvert \le 4\), write \(-4\le x+1\le 4\), so \(-5\le x\le 3\). An equation asks for boundary distances; a less-than inequality includes the numbers between the boundaries.

activity.prompt: What is the sum of all real solutions to \(\lvert 2 x-5\rvert =9\)?
activity.explanation: The two branches give \(x=7\) and \(x=-2\). Their sum is 5. Using only the positive branch misses a real solution; the number inside an absolute value is allowed to be negative.

title: Clear denominators while protecting the original domain

section.heading: Clear denominators while protecting the original domain
body: Exclude every input making an original denominator zero. Factor before canceling: only multiplied factors cancel across a fraction. Multiply by a common denominator to clear a rational equation, then solve the resulting equation and check candidates in the original. A quadratic may require the formula \(x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{b^{2}-4 ac}}{2 a}\); its roots sum to \(\frac{-b}{a}\).

Difference of squares uses \(u^{2}-v^{2}=\left(u-v\right) \left(u+v\right)\). A monic quadratic \(x^{2}+bx+c\) factors by finding numbers adding to b and multiplying to c. Factor numerators and denominators with these rules before canceling.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\frac{2}{x-1}+\frac{2}{x+1}=1\), first exclude \(x=\pm 1\). Multiplying by \(x^{2}-1\) gives \(4 x=x^{2}-1\), or \(x^{2}-4 x-1=0\). The roots are \(2\pm \sqrt{5}\), neither excluded, so their sum is 4. Cancellation never makes an originally forbidden input valid.

activity.prompt: Which x satisfies \(\frac{x^{2}-25}{x-5}=12\)?
activity.explanation: Exclude \(x=5\), then factor the numerator as (x−5)(x+5). The allowed equation becomes \(x+5=12\), giving \(x=7\). The candidate 5 is undefined in the original expression; 17 reverses the final subtraction.

title: Use roots, coefficients, and integer factor pairs

section.heading: Use roots, coefficients, and integer factor pairs
body: For \(ax^{2}+bx+c\) with \(a\ne 0\), roots r, s satisfy \(r+s=\frac{-b}{a}\) and \(rs=\frac{c}{a}\). With known roots write a(x−r)(x−s), then use a point to find a. A stated zero can be substituted to determine a missing coefficient. Use \(\left(r+s\right)^{2}=r^{2}+2 rs+s^{2}\) for squared-root sums. Positive integer roots must be positive factor pairs of their product.

The square identity applies to any numbers, not only named roots. If \(x+\frac{1}{x}=6\) with \(x\ne 0\), its square gives \(x^{2}+2+\frac{1}{x^{2}}=36\), so the requested square sum is 34. For \(x-\frac{1}{x}=3\), the cross term is−2 and the square sum is 11.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Zeros 2 and 7 with \(p \left(0\right)=28\) give \(p \left(x\right)=a \left(x-2\right) \left(x-7\right)\) and \(14 a=28\), so \(a=2\). The roots sum to 9 and multiply to 14; their squares sum to \(9^{2}-2 \left(14\right)=53\). If two distinct positive integer roots multiply to 18, the pairs (1, 18), (2, 9), (3, 6) yield possible sums 19, 11, 9.

activity.prompt: If \(x^{2}-kx+20=0\) has distinct positive integer roots, what is the sum of all possible k values?
activity.explanation: The factor pairs of 20 are (1, 20), (2, 10), (4, 5), giving \(k=21\), 12, 9. Add these possible coefficients to obtain 42. Do not add root products or count the same unordered pair twice.

title: Solve simple and compound linear inequalities

section.heading: Solve simple and compound linear inequalities
body: Add or subtract the same quantity on both sides as for an equation. Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality. In a compound inequality, perform an operation on all three parts and preserve which endpoints are strict. Check a test value to verify the direction of your answer.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(-4 \left(2 x-1\right)\le 20\), expand to \(-8 x+4\le 20\), so \(-8 x\le 16\). Dividing by −8 gives \(x\ge -2\). For \(-1<2 x+3\le 9\), subtract 3 throughout and divide by positive \(2:-2<x\le 3\). The lower endpoint remains excluded while the upper stays included.

activity.prompt: Which inequality is equivalent to \(-3 x+6>15\)?
activity.explanation: Subtract 6 to get \(-3 x>9\). Dividing by −3 reverses the sign: \(x<-3\). A check with \(x=-4\) gives \(18>15\); \(x=0\) does not work.

title: Use the discriminant and the complete quadratic formula

section.heading: Use the discriminant and the complete quadratic formula
body: Put a quadratic into \(ax^{2}+bx+c=0\) before reading its coefficients. With \(a\ne 0\), \(D=b^{2}-4 ac\) determines the number of real roots: \(D>0\) gives two, \(D=0\) one repeated root, and \(D<0\) none. The complete formula is \(x=\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{D}}{2 a}\). A parameter condition such as \(k>0\) may select one sign of a coefficient.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(x^{2}-6 x+2=0\), \(D=36-8=28\), so \(x=\frac{6\pm \sqrt{28}}{2}=3\pm \sqrt{7}\). Completing the square confirms \(\left(x-3\right)^{2}=7\). For \(3 x^{2}+kx+12=0\) to have one real root, \(k^{2}-144=0\); if k is negative, \(k=-12\), giving \(3 \left(x-2\right)^{2}\).

activity.prompt: For which positive k does \(x^{2}+kx+25=0\) have one real solution?
activity.explanation: A repeated real root requires \(k^{2}-100=0\). The positive condition selects \(k=10\); the equation then becomes \(\left(x+5\right)^{2}=0\). The coefficient k is not the root or the constant term.

title: Expand, factor, and count real polynomial zeros

section.heading: Expand, factor, and count real polynomial zeros
body: Distribute all products when expanding; the x term in a binomial product usually receives two contributions. To factor, take out common factors, group common binomials, and use \(u^{2}-v^{2}=\left(u-v\right) \left(u+v\right)\). A factor gives a real zero only if its equation has a real solution; a polynomial degree does not guarantee that many real roots.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Expand \(\left(3 x-2\right) \left(x+4\right)=3 x^{2}+10 x-8\). For \(x^{3}+x^{2}-16 x-16\), group \(x^{2} \left(x+1\right)-16 \left(x+1\right)=\left(x+1\right) \left(x-4\right) \left(x+4\right)\). The real zeros are −1, 4, −4. In \(x^{4}-81=\left(x^{2}-9\right) \left(x^{2}+9\right)\), only \(x=\pm 3\) are real; \(x^{2}=-9\) has no real solution.

activity.prompt: What is the largest real zero of \(x^{3}-2 x^{2}-9 x+18\)?
activity.explanation: Group \(x^{2} \left(x-2\right)-9 \left(x-2\right)=\left(x-2\right) \left(x-3\right) \left(x+3\right)\). The real zeros are 2, 3, −3, so the largest is 3. The number 9 is the squared factor, not a zero.

title: Evaluate the remainder without dividing the polynomial

section.heading: Evaluate the remainder without dividing the polynomial
body: When dividing P(x) by x−r, the remainder is P(r). Set the divisor equal to zero to identify r, so x+a uses \(r=-a\). A remainder of zero means the divisor is a factor; a nonzero remainder does not. Keep parentheses around a negative substituted input and apply the whole power before multiplying.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(P \left(x\right)=x^{3}+2 x^{2}-5\), division by x+2 uses \(r=-2\). Then \(P \left(-2\right)=-8+8-5=-5\). Dividing by x−1 would instead leave \(P \left(1\right)=1+2-5=-2\). The sign comes from the divisor, not from choosing whichever input is easier.

activity.prompt: What is the remainder when \(2 x^{3}+x-4\) is divided by x+1?
activity.explanation: The divisor vanishes at \(x=-1\). Evaluate \(2 \left(-1\right)^{3}+\left(-1\right)-4=-2-1-4=-7\). Substituting +1 gives −1, which is the remainder for the different divisor x−1.

title: Combine rational expressions before canceling

section.heading: Combine rational expressions before canceling
body: Use a common denominator before adding or subtracting fractions with variables. Multiply each numerator by its missing denominator factor. For a complex fraction, simplify its numerator and denominator separately, then multiply by the reciprocal of the entire denominator. State nonzero denominators first; never cancel terms joined by addition.

A monic quadratic \(x^{2}+bx+c\) factors as(x+m)(x+n)when \(m+n=b\) and \(mn=c\). For \(a^{2}-b^{2}\), use(a−b)(a+b). These factorizations let you cancel a common whole factor while preserving the original excluded inputs.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(x\ne \pm 2\), \(\frac{1}{x+2}+\frac{4}{x-2}=\frac{\left(x-2\right)+4 \left(x+2\right)}{x^{2}-4}=\frac{5 x+6}{x^{2}-4}\). For nonzero a, b with \(a\ne 2 b\), the complex fraction \(\frac{\frac{2}{a}+\frac{1}{b}}{\frac{2}{a}-\frac{1}{b}}\) becomes \(\frac{\frac{2 b+a}{ab}}{\frac{2 b-a}{ab}}=\frac{2 b+a}{2 b-a}\). The subtraction order survives cancellation.

activity.prompt: For \(x\ne 0\), −1, which numerator results when \(\frac{2}{x}+\frac{3}{x+1}\) is combined over x(x+1)?
activity.explanation: The combined numerator is \(2 \left(x+1\right)+3 x=5 x+2\). Adding only the variable terms drops the constant; using 3 as the constant attaches the wrong numerator to the missing factor.

title: Solve product and rational inequalities with a sign chart

section.heading: Solve product and rational inequalities with a sign chart
body: Factor the expression and mark every numerator zero and denominator zero on a number line. Test one input in each interval, then keep intervals with the requested sign. Include a numerator zero for \(\le\) or \(\ge\), but exclude every original denominator zero. A canceled factor remains excluded. Do not multiply by an unknown-sign denominator without splitting cases.

For a monic quadratic \(x^{2}+bx+c\), look for numbers m and n with \(m+n=b\) and \(mn=c\), giving(x+m)(x+n). Apply this to both numerator and denominator before choosing test intervals; retain a canceled denominator zero as an excluded input.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\frac{x-1}{x+3}\ge 0\), critical inputs are −3 and 1. Test \(x=-4\), 0, 2 to obtain positive, negative, positive. The solution is \(x<-3\) or \(x\ge 1:1\) is included and −3 is not. For a quadratic product \(\left(x+2\right) \left(x-5\right)\le 0\), the negative region lies between its zeros, including both endpoints.

activity.prompt: Which is the solution to \(\frac{x+4}{x-2}<0\)?
activity.explanation: The signs differ only between the critical inputs −4 and 2. Both endpoints are excluded: the numerator equals zero at −4 but the sign must be strictly negative, and the denominator is undefined at 2.

title: Keep valid signs when squaring a radical equation

section.heading: Keep valid signs when squaring a radical equation
body: A principal square root is nonnegative. In \(\sqrt{u}=v\), require both \(u\ge 0\) and \(v\ge 0\) before squaring to obtain \(u=v^{2}\). Isolate a radical first, solve the squared equation, and substitute every candidate into the original. Squaring can preserve a false negative branch; passing the squared equation alone is not sufficient.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\sqrt{3 x+4}=x\), the original right side requires \(x\ge 0\). Squaring gives \(x^{2}-3 x-4=\left(x-4\right) \left(x+1\right)=0\). Candidate 4 works because \(\sqrt{16}=4\), but −1 fails because \(\sqrt{1}=1\ne -1\). The sign restriction lets you reject the extraneous candidate before unnecessary calculation.

activity.prompt: Which solution of \(x^{2}-2 x-8=0\) also satisfies \(\sqrt{2 x+8}=x\)?
activity.explanation: The squared equation factors as \(\left(x-4\right) \left(x+2\right)=0\). The original square root cannot equal −2, while \(x=4\) gives \(\sqrt{16}=4\). Therefore only 4 survives.

title: Use exponent laws and a common base

section.heading: Use exponent laws and a common base
body: Multiplying powers with the same nonzero base adds exponents; dividing subtracts them. Raising a power to a power multiplies exponents. A negative integer exponent means reciprocal, not a negative number. Rewrite both sides of an exponential equation with the same positive base other than 1 before equating exponents.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\left(a^{-3} b^{2}\right)^{2}\), distribute the outside power: \(a^{-6} b^{4}=\frac{b^{4}}{a^{6}}\), with \(a\ne 0\). In \(4^{x-1}=32\), rewrite \(4=2^{2}\) and \(32=2^{5}\), giving \(2 x-2=5\) and \(x=\frac{7}{2}\). The exponent applies to the whole grouped expression.

activity.explanation: Write \(27=3^{3}\), so \(2 x-1=3\) and \(2 x=4\). Thus \(x=2\). Equating x itself to the exponent 3 ignores the rest of the exponent expression.

title: Distinguish identities, contradictions, and matching coefficients

section.heading: Distinguish identities, contradictions, and matching coefficients
body: After simplifying a linear equation \(Ax=B\), \(A\ne 0\) gives one solution, \(A=0\) with \(B\ne 0\) gives none, and \(A=B=0\) gives infinitely many. An identity must hold for every allowed input: expand both sides and match each power’s coefficient. A single input cannot prove an identity unless the remaining expression is already constant.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\left(k+4\right) x=0\), \(k=-4\) makes the equation true for every x. If instead the right side were 7, the same k would give no solution. In \(a \left(x-1\right)^{2}+b=ax^{2}-10 x+9\), compare linear coefficients \(-2 a=-10\) to find \(a=5\), then constants \(a+b=9\) give \(b=4\).

activity.prompt: For which k does \(\left(k-5\right) x=8\) have no solution for x?
activity.explanation: An equation with a nonzero x coefficient has one solution. It is impossible only when \(k-5=0\), giving \(0=8\). Hence \(k=5\); this does not mean that x itself must equal zero.

title: Intersect the restrictions of the actual inputs

section.heading: Intersect the restrictions of the actual inputs
body: A real square root permits a nonnegative radicand; a logarithm requires a strictly positive argument; every denominator must be nonzero. For a composition, apply each restriction to the input actually received by that function. Intersect all conditions rather than choosing the most restrictive-looking endpoint. Check whether equality is allowed at a boundary.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(u\right)=\frac{1}{u-5}\) and \(g \left(x\right)=\sqrt{x+4}\), g requires \(x\ge -4\). The outer denominator requires \(\sqrt{x+4}\ne 5\), excluding \(x=21\). Thus the composition permits \(x\ge -4\) except 21. At the lower endpoint, \(g \left(-4\right)=0\) and the denominator is −5, so the endpoint is allowed.

activity.prompt: What is the domain of \(\frac{\sqrt{9-x}}{x+1}\)?
activity.explanation: The radicand requires \(x\le 9\), including 9 because a zero square root is allowed. The denominator excludes \(x=-1\). Restricting to \(x<9\) loses a valid endpoint; excluding 1 uses the wrong sign for the denominator zero.

title: Evaluate nested functions in the correct order

section.heading: Evaluate nested functions in the correct order
body: In f(g(x)), g acts first and its output becomes the entire input to f. A nested inverse asks for an input producing a named output: solve \(f \left(t\right)=y\) to obtain f⁻¹(y). An added term inside the outer function prevents immediate inverse cancellation. Write each intermediate input explicitly; composition is not multiplication.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Let \(f \left(x\right)=2 x-5\) and \(g \left(x\right)=x^{2}+1\). Then \(f \left(g \left(3\right)\right)=f \left(10\right)=15\), while \(g \left(f \left(3\right)\right)=g \left(1\right)=2\). For f(f⁻¹(7)+4), first solve \(2 t-5=7\) to get \(t=6\); the outer input is 10 and the final value is 15. The extra 4 sits between the two operations.

activity.prompt: If \(f \left(x\right)=x^{2}+2\) and \(g \left(x\right)=2 x-1\), what is f(g(3))?
activity.explanation: The inner value is \(g \left(3\right)=5\), then \(f \left(5\right)=25+2=27\). Reversing the order gives \(g \left(f \left(3\right)\right)=g \left(11\right)=21\). Multiplying the separate outputs gives \(f \left(3\right) g \left(3\right)=11\cdot 5=55\), a different operation.

title: Calculate function differences and average rates

section.heading: Calculate function differences and average rates
body: Average rate of change is \(\frac{f \left(b\right)-f \left(a\right)}{b-a}\), with \(a\ne b\). Evaluate both outputs and preserve the same subtraction order in numerator and denominator. For f(x+h)−f(x), substitute x+h into every x, expand, and subtract the entire original expression. A difference quotient additionally divides by nonzero h; it is not simply f(h).

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(f \left(x\right)=x^{2}+3\), outputs at 1 and 4 are 4 and 19, giving average rate \(\frac{19-4}{4-1}=5\). Algebraically, \(f \left(x+h\right)-f \left(x\right)=\left(x+h\right)^{2}+3-\left(x^{2}+3\right)=2 xh+h^{2}\). Dividing by \(h\ne 0\) gives 2 x+h. The constant terms cancel, while the cross term 2 xh remains.

activity.prompt: For \(f \left(x\right)=x^{2}-4 x\), what is its average rate from \(x=1\) to \(x=5\)?
activity.explanation: \(f \left(1\right)=-3\) and \(f \left(5\right)=5\). The output change 8 divided by input change 4 gives 2. Reporting 8 gives only a change, while dividing by the final input 5 uses the wrong interval.

title: Find an inverse value on the allowed branch

section.heading: Find an inverse value on the allowed branch
body: An inverse value f⁻¹(y) asks which original input gives output y. Solve \(f \left(x\right)=y\), then use the original domain to select a branch and check denominators. The inverse of a quadratic is a function only after a one-to-one domain is chosen. The notation f⁻¹ is not a reciprocal.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(x\right)=\left(x-4\right)^{2}+2\) with \(x\ge 4\), finding f⁻¹(18) gives \(\left(x-4\right)^{2}=16\) and candidates 0 or 8. Only 8 is allowed; \(f \left(8\right)=18\). For \(f \left(x\right)=\frac{2 x+1}{x-3}\), an inverse value 3 solves \(2 x+1=3 x-9\), giving 10, whose denominator 7 is nonzero.

activity.prompt: If \(f \left(x\right)=\left(x+2\right)^{2}-1\) for \(x\le -2\), what is f⁻¹(8)?
activity.explanation: Solve \(\left(x+2\right)^{2}=9\), giving \(x=1\) or−5. The domain \(x\le -2\) selects−5. The value−3 would make \(f \left(x\right)=0\), not 8; the positive branch is outside the domain.

title: Move a feature by solving for its new input

section.heading: Move a feature by solving for its new input
body: If \(g \left(x\right)=af \left(bx+c\right)+d\), an original point(u, v) moves to \(\left(\frac{u-c}{b},av+d\right)\), with \(b\ne 0\). Solve \(bx+c=u\) instead of guessing the horizontal direction. A quadratic vertex lies halfway between its zeros; in \(a \left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\) it is(h, k). An absolute-value vertex occurs where its inside equals zero.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Suppose f has vertex(6, −2) and \(g \left(x\right)=-2 f \left(3 x-3\right)+1\). Solve \(3 x-3=6\) to find \(x=3\); transform the output to \(-2 \left(-2\right)+1=5\). Thus g has vertex(3, 5). For a quadratic with zeros 2 and 8 and minimum−4, the original vertex is(5, −4) before any transformation.

activity.prompt: f has a zero at input 9. If \(g \left(x\right)=f \left(2 x+1\right)\), where is the corresponding zero of g?
activity.explanation: The supplied input to f must equal \(9:2 x+1=9\), hence \(x=4\). The other choices add the horizontal constant or apply the input multiplier in the wrong direction.

title: Use logarithm laws without losing the domain

section.heading: Use logarithm laws without losing the domain
body: For \(b>0\), \(b\ne 1\), \(\log _{b}\left(u\right)=v\) means \(u=b^{v}\) and requires \(u>0\). Products inside a log become sums; quotients become differences. These laws do not split a sum inside a logarithm. In an equation with several logs, state positivity for each original argument before combining, then reject candidates violating it.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\log _{2}\left(x-2\right)+\log _{2}\left(x+2\right)=5\), require \(x>2\). Combining gives \(\log _{2}\left(x^{2}-4\right)=5\), hence \(x^{2}=36\). The allowed root is 6; −6 fails the original arguments. Separately, \(\log _{3}\left(a\right)=2\) and \(\log _{3}\left(b\right)=4\) imply \(\log _{3}\left(ab\right)=6\) by adding, not multiplying, the two logs.

activity.prompt: What is the real solution to \(\log _{2}\left(x+1\right)=4\)?
activity.explanation: The logarithm definition gives \(x+1=2^{4}=16\), so \(x=15\). This makes the argument 16 positive. The value 16 is the argument, not x; multiplying the base by the exponent is not the definition.

title: Count the jumps in an arithmetic sequence

section.heading: Count the jumps in an arithmetic sequence
body: An arithmetic sequence adds a constant difference d. If indexing starts at 0, \(a_{n}=a_{0}+nd\); if it starts at 1, \(a_{n}=a_{1}+\left(n-1\right) d\). Find d from two consecutive terms and count jumps from the explicitly named first index. A decreasing sequence has a negative difference, which stays negative when substituted.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(a_{0}=53\) and \(a_{1}=46\), the common difference is−7. Thus \(a_{5}=53+5 \left(-7\right)=18\). The list 53, 46, 39, 32, 25, 18 contains six terms but only five jumps. Using four jumps would give \(a_{4}=25\), which is a different requested index.

activity.prompt: An arithmetic sequence has \(a_{0}=31\) and \(a_{1}=26\). What is \(a_{4}\)?
activity.explanation: The difference is \(26-31=-5\). Four jumps from index 0 give \(a_{4}=31-20=11\). Three jumps give 16, and five jumps give 6; both are indexing errors.

title: Follow a recurrence with more than one input

section.heading: Follow a recurrence with more than one input
body: A function of two variables has two input slots; substitute each value into its own slot. A recurrence gives the next sequence term from the previous term and may also use the step number. Start from the stated initial term, calculate one step at a time, and update both inputs. Squaring a negative previous term makes a positive square.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Let \(F \left(x,y\right)=2 x+y\) and \(a_{0}=3\), with \(a_{n+1}=F \left(a_{n},n+1\right)\). At \(n=0\), \(a_{1}=F \left(3,1\right)=7\). At \(n=1\), \(a_{2}=F \left(7,2\right)=16\). At \(n=2\), \(a_{3}=F \left(16,3\right)=35\). The second input is 1, then 2, then 3; it does not stay fixed at the original index.

activity.explanation: At \(n=0\), \(b_{1}=2^{2}-0=4\). Then \(n=1\) gives \(b_{2}=4^{2}-1=15\). Reusing \(n=0\) gives 16; applying the recurrence only once does not produce the second term.

title: Choose the piece from the input before calculating

section.heading: Choose the piece from the input before calculating
body: A piecewise function assigns different formulas to different input conditions. Locate the input in exactly one condition, including whether an endpoint uses \(<\) or \(\le\), then evaluate only that formula. The size or sign of a calculated output does not decide which branch applies. Check the condition before doing arithmetic.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(x\right)=2 x-3\) when \(x<1\) and \(f \left(x\right)=x^{2}+4\) when \(x\ge 1\), input−2 uses the first branch and gives−7. Input 1 uses the second branch, giving 5, because the equality sign belongs to \(x\ge 1\). The first branch’s value−1 at 1 is irrelevant: that branch is not defined there.

activity.prompt: For \(f \left(x\right)=3 x+2\) when \(x<0\) and \(f \left(x\right)=x^{2}-5\) when \(x\ge 0\), what is f(0)?
activity.explanation: The boundary 0 meets \(x\ge 0\), so use \(0^{2}-5=-5\). Using the other branch would produce 2 but violates its strict condition \(x<0\). Choose the rule from the input, then calculate.

title: Find possible outputs from a quadratic vertex

section.heading: Find possible outputs from a quadratic vertex
body: Range describes possible outputs, not allowed inputs. In \(f \left(x\right)=a \left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\) over all real x, the square is nonnegative. If \(a>0\), the least output is k and \(y\ge k\); if \(a<0\), the greatest is k and \(y\le k\). The equality endpoint is attained at \(x=h\). A restricted domain may change the range, so inspect it first.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(x\right)=-4 \left(x-3\right)^{2}+11\) on all real x, the squared contribution is at most zero after multiplication by−4. Thus the maximum is 11, reached at \(x=3\), and the range is \(y\le 11\). The number 3 locates the vertex horizontally; it is not a range endpoint.

activity.prompt: What is the range of \(f \left(x\right)=2 \left(x+5\right)^{2}-7\) on all real x?
activity.explanation: The positive multiple of a square is nonnegative, so the minimum output is−7 at \(x=-5\). Therefore \(y\ge -7\). The input−5 and output−7 have different roles.

title: Distinguish holes, asymptotes, and excluded outputs

section.heading: Distinguish holes, asymptotes, and excluded outputs
body: Factor a rational function before interpreting its graph. An original denominator zero remains forbidden. If its factor cancels and the reduced function is finite there, the graph has a hole; an uncanceled denominator zero with nonzero numerator gives a vertical asymptote. To test an excluded output, set \(y=f \left(x\right)\), solve for x, and identify output values making that equation impossible.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(x\right)=\frac{x^{2}-49}{x-7}\), cancellation leaves x+7 for \(x\ne 7\), producing a hole at(7, 14). The function \(\frac{1}{x-6}\) instead has a vertical asymptote at \(x=6\). For \(g \left(x\right)=\frac{x+4}{x-2}\), rearranging gives \(x \left(y-1\right)=2 y+4\); output \(y=1\) would require \(0=6\), so it is never produced.

activity.prompt: Where is the hole of \(f \left(x\right)=\frac{x^{2}-64}{x-8}\)?
activity.explanation: The reduced line is x+8, but input 8 remains excluded. Its missing point would have output 16, so the hole is(8, 16). The point(−8, 0) is an ordinary allowed zero, not the excluded input.

title: Tell additive, quadratic, and exponential patterns apart

section.heading: Tell additive, quadratic, and exponential patterns apart
body: At equal input steps, linear outputs have constant first differences, quadratic outputs have constant second differences, and exponential outputs have constant ratios. For \(f \left(t\right)=ab^{t}\) with a, \(b>0\), \(\frac{f(v)}{f(u)}=b^{v-u}\); use the input gap before finding b. Half-life h gives \(a \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{h}}\). A pattern explicitly stated to be quadratic or exponential fixes how it continues.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: An exponential function has \(f \left(1\right)=21\) and \(f \left(3\right)=189\). The ratio 9 spans two steps, so \(b^{2}=9\) and \(b=3\); the initial coefficient is \(a=7\). In a quadratic table 1, 5, 13, 25 at inputs 0, 1, 2, 3, differences 4, 8, 12 have constant difference 4, so the next output is \(25+16=41\).

activity.prompt: A quantity starts at 160 and halves every 3 hours. How much remains after 9 hours?
activity.explanation: Nine hours contain 3 half-life periods, giving \(160 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}=20\). Counting only two halvings gives 40. The exponent counts periods, not the raw hours.

title: Test symmetry by substituting a negative input

section.heading: Test symmetry by substituting a negative input
body: An even function satisfies \(f \left(-x\right)=f \left(x\right)\), giving y-axis symmetry. An odd function satisfies \(f \left(-x\right)=-f \left(x\right)\), giving origin symmetry. The domain must contain both x and−x. For a polynomial, even powers and a constant can form an even function; only odd powers with zero constant can form an odd function. Mixed powers usually give neither.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(x\right)=2 x^{6}-x^{2}+8\), replacing x by−x leaves every term unchanged, so f is even. For \(g \left(x\right)=x^{5}-4 x\), every term changes sign, so g is odd. Adding a nonzero constant to g destroys odd symmetry even though its variable powers remain odd.

activity.prompt: Which polynomial is odd?
activity.explanation: The expression \(2 x^{5}-3 x\) changes sign completely when x becomes−x, so it is odd. The constant in \(x^{3}+2\) does not change sign, while \(x^{4}-x^{2}\) is even rather than odd.

title: Solve graph crossings and locate negative outputs

section.heading: Solve graph crossings and locate negative outputs
body: Graphs intersect where their outputs are equal: solve \(f \left(x\right)=g \left(x\right)\). Zeros are intersections with \(y=0\). Move everything to one side, factor or use the quadratic formula, and preserve a possible zero input before dividing by x. To locate negative outputs of an upward quadratic, use the real roots as boundaries and test the intervals.

To factor \(x^{2}+bx+c\), find two numbers adding to b and multiplying to c. Their factors locate the roots, after which one test point in each interval determines the sign. A repeated root touches the axis without necessarily changing sign.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: The curves \(y=x^{2}\) and \(y=3 x+4\) intersect when \(x^{2}-3 x-4=\left(x-4\right) \left(x+1\right)=0\), giving inputs 4 and−1 with sum 3. For \(f \left(x\right)=\left(x-1\right) \left(x-6\right)\), a test input 3 gives a negative product, while outside inputs give positive products. Thus \(f \left(x\right)<0\) for \(1<x<6\).

activity.prompt: What is the sum of the x-coordinates where \(y=x^{2}\) and \(y=4 x\) intersect?
activity.explanation: Solve \(x^{2}-4 x=x \left(x-4\right)=0\). The two input coordinates are 0 and 4, whose sum is 4. Dividing by x without checking zero would discard one crossing, and 16 is an output rather than the requested sum.

title: Keep the product fixed in inverse variation

section.heading: Keep the product fixed in inverse variation
body: Inverse variation has \(y=\frac{k}{x}\) with \(x\ne 0\), so the product xy stays constant. Use a known pair to determine k, then divide it by the new input. For positive values, increasing the input decreases the output. This is different from direct variation \(y=kx\), which keeps a ratio constant instead of a product.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(f \left(3\right)=20\) and f varies inversely, \(k=3\cdot 20=60\). Thus \(f \left(12\right)=\frac{60}{12}=5\). The input became four times as large, so the output becomes one fourth as large. Using \(f \left(12\right)=80\) would apply direct variation and increase both quantities.

activity.prompt: If f varies inversely and \(f \left(4\right)=18\), what is f(9)?
activity.explanation: The constant product is \(4\cdot 18=72\). At input 9, the output is \(\frac{72}{9}=8\). The 40.5 choice uses a constant ratio rather than a constant product; subtraction does not model inverse variation.

title: Average parallel bases and use perpendicular height

section.heading: Average parallel bases and use perpendicular height
body: A trapezoid’s area is \(A=\frac{\left(b_{1}+b_{2}\right) h}{2}\), where \(b_{1}\), \(b_{2}\) are its parallel bases and h is the distance between their lines at a right angle. A slanted side is not the height. Convert all lengths to the same unit first and report square units. Averaging the bases avoids treating the whole shape as the larger bounding rectangle.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: With bases 7 and 17 and perpendicular height 6, average the bases to 12 and multiply by 6: area 72 square units. A slanted side of length 10 does not replace the height. Computing \(17\cdot 6=102\) uses only the larger base and includes extra space outside the trapezoid.

activity.prompt: A trapezoid has bases 5 and 15 and perpendicular height 8. What is its area?
activity.explanation: The average base is \(\frac{5+15}{2}=10\). Multiply by 8 to obtain 80 square units. Using only the smaller or larger base gives the other two options.

title: Include the cylinder’s curved side and both ends

section.heading: Include the cylinder’s curved side and both ends
body: A closed right circular cylinder has total surface area \(2 \pi  rh+2 \pi  r^{2}\). The first term is the curved side, obtained by unrolling it into a rectangle with width equal to the circumference. The second includes two circular ends. An open container may have fewer ends; read which surfaces are exposed. Volume \(\pi  r^{2} h\) has cubic units and is a different quantity.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For radius 2 and height 9, the curved area is \(2 \pi \cdot 2\cdot 9=36 \pi\). The two ends contribute \(2 \pi \cdot 2^{2}=8 \pi\), so closed surface area is \(44 \pi\) square units. Leaving out the ends gives only the lateral area; \(\pi \cdot 2^{2}\cdot 9=36 \pi\) happens to have the same coefficient here but measures volume.

activity.prompt: What is the total surface area of a closed cylinder with radius 5 and height 3?
activity.explanation: The curved side is \(2 \pi \cdot 5\cdot 3=30 \pi\) and the two ends add \(2 \pi \cdot 25=50 \pi\). Total \(80 \pi\) square units includes all three surfaces. The \(75 \pi\) choice is the volume coefficient.

title: Find triangle area from three sides

section.heading: Find triangle area from three sides
body: When all three side lengths are known but no perpendicular height is given, use Heron’s formula: \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}\) and \(A=\sqrt{s \left(s-a\right) \left(s-b\right) \left(s-c\right)}\). Check the triangle inequality first. Do not use a slanted side as a height. The result has square units; the semiperimeter s is half the perimeter, not the full perimeter.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A triangle with sides 10, 10, 12 has semiperimeter 16. Thus \(A=\sqrt{16\cdot 6\cdot 6\cdot 4}=\sqrt{2304}=48\). Its altitude to base 12 is \(\sqrt{10^{2}-6^{2}}=8\), independently confirming \(\frac{12\cdot 8}{2}=48\). Both approaches account for the perpendicular height rather than multiplying two arbitrary side lengths.

activity.prompt: What is the area of a triangle with sides 5, 5, 8?
activity.explanation: The semiperimeter is 9, so Heron gives \(\sqrt{9\cdot 4\cdot 4\cdot 1}=12\). Equivalently, half the base is 4 and the altitude is 3, giving \(\frac{8\cdot 3}{2}=12\).

title: Match chord parts and whole secants correctly

section.heading: Match chord parts and whole secants correctly
body: Intersecting chords inside a circle satisfy \(\left(p_{1}\right) \left(p_{2}\right)=\left(p_{3}\right) \left(p_{4}\right)\), pairing segments on the same chord. From an external point, two secants satisfy \(o_1w_1=o_2w_2\), and a tangent has \(t^2=ow\). Add the outside and inside portions to obtain the whole secant. Lengths are positive, so take the positive square root for a tangent.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If crossing chords have parts 2 and 18 on one chord and 3 and x on the other, \(36=3 x\) gives \(x=12\). For a tangent paired with a secant whose outside is 4 and inside is 5, the whole is 9: \(t^2=4\cdot 9=36\), so the tangent is 6. Using \(4\cdot 5\) would incorrectly omit the outside part from the whole.

activity.prompt: Two secants share an outside point. One has outside 4 and whole 15; the other has outside 5 and whole x. What is x?
activity.explanation: Equal products give \(4\cdot 15=5 x\), so \(x=12\). This is the whole second secant; its inside portion would be \(12-5=7\), a different length.

title: Locate the vertex before using an intercepted arc

section.heading: Locate the vertex before using an intercepted arc
body: A central angle equals its intercepted arc measure. An inscribed angle with vertex on the circle is half its intercepted arc. Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to \(180^\circ\). For two chords crossing inside, the angle is half the sum of the opposite intercepted arcs; for an outside secant or tangent angle, use half their difference. Identify the vertex location and the relevant arcs before calculating.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: An inscribed angle intercepting \(a 132^\circ\) arc measures \(66^\circ\). The central angle for that arc would measure \(132^\circ\). In a cyclic quadrilateral, an interior angle \(104^\circ\) forces its opposite to \(76^\circ\). The angles are opposite, not merely adjacent; an arbitrary quadrilateral need not have this supplementary relationship.

activity.prompt: An inscribed angle intercepts \(a 118^\circ\) arc. What is the angle?
activity.explanation: The on-circle vertex makes the angle half the intercepted arc: \(\frac{118}{2}=59^\circ\). The \(118^\circ\) option treats it as central; \(62^\circ\) comes from subtracting the arc from \(180^\circ\) instead of halving it.

title: Normalize a line equation to find the shortest distance

section.heading: Normalize a line equation to find the shortest distance
body: The perpendicular distance from \(\left(x_{0},y_{0}\right)\) to \(Ax+By+C=0\) is \(\frac{\lvert Ax_{0}+By_{0}+C\rvert }{\sqrt{A^{2}+B^{2}}}\), provided A and B are not both zero. Put all terms on one side first. The denominator normalizes the line’s coefficients; an x- or y-intercept is generally not a perpendicular distance. The absolute value makes the result nonnegative.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: To find the distance from(1, 2) to \(5 x+12 y-3=0\), substitute to obtain \(\frac{\lvert 5+24-3\rvert }{\sqrt{169}}=\frac{26}{13}=2\). Multiplying every line coefficient by the same nonzero constant changes neither the line nor the distance because numerator and denominator scale equally.

activity.prompt: What is the distance from the origin to \(8 x+15 y=34\)?
activity.explanation: Write \(8 x+15 y-34=0\). The distance is \(\frac{34}{\sqrt{64+225}}=\frac{34}{17}=2\). The other options are intercept distances measured along coordinate axes, not the shortest perpendicular segment.

title: Separate length, area, and volume scale factors

section.heading: Separate length, area, and volume scale factors
body: For similar figures, a corresponding length scale factor k multiplies every length and perimeter by k, every area by \(k^{2}\), and every volume by \(k^{3}\). Recover k with a square root from an area ratio or a cube root from a volume ratio. State which direction the ratio compares. Similarity requires the same shape, not merely one matching dimension.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If similar triangles have area ratio 25: 64, their length ratio is 5: 8. A smaller perimeter 30 becomes \(\frac{30\cdot 8}{5}=48\). If similar solids have heights 3 and 6, their length factor is 2 and a smaller volume 11 becomes \(11\cdot 2^{3}=88\). Multiplying a volume by 2 would scale only one dimension.

activity.prompt: Similar solids have volume ratio 27: 125. What is the corresponding smaller-to-larger length ratio?
activity.explanation: Cube roots recover the length ratio: \(\sqrt[3]{27}:\sqrt[3]{125}=3:5\). The ratio 9: 25 is the associated area ratio; 27: 125 is still a volume ratio.

title: Convert the central-angle fraction to arc or sector

section.heading: Convert the central-angle fraction to arc or sector
body: A central angle \(\theta\) in degrees occupies \(\frac{\theta }{360}\) of a circle. Its arc length is \(\left(\frac{\theta }{360}\right) 2 \pi  r\); its sector area is \(\left(\frac{\theta }{360}\right) \pi  r^{2}\). In radians the formulas become \(\text{arc}=r \theta\) and \(\text{sector}=\frac{r^{2} \theta }{2}\). Identify whether the target is a distance or an area, and never insert a degree value into a radian formula.

A full circle has circumference \(2 \pi  r\) and area \(\pi  r^{2}\). If the circumference is \(14 \pi\), then \(r=7\) and the area \(49 \pi\); solve for the radius before switching from a length measurement to an area.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For radius 8 and central angle \(135^\circ\), the angle fraction is \(\frac{3}{8}\). Arc length is \(\left(\frac{3}{8}\right) \left(16 \pi \right)=6 \pi\), while sector area is \(\left(\frac{3}{8}\right) \left(64 \pi \right)=24 \pi\). These quantities use the same fraction but different whole-circle measures. The angle is also \(\frac{3 \pi }{4}\) radians, giving the same results.

activity.prompt: What is the arc length for radius 10 and central angle \(54^\circ\)?
activity.explanation: The arc is \(\frac{54}{360}=\frac{3}{20}\) of circumference \(20 \pi\), giving \(3 \pi\). The \(15 \pi\) choice is sector area for the same circle; \(6 \pi\) can result from doubling the circumference factor twice.

title: Build the right triangle hidden in a circle

section.heading: Build the right triangle hidden in a circle
body: A radius to a tangent point is perpendicular to the tangent. The center’s perpendicular to a chord bisects the chord, giving a right triangle with half-chord as a leg. An inscribed rectangle’s diagonal is the circle’s diameter. Use \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\) with the radius or diagonal in its actual role. A triangle area needs half of base times its perpendicular height, not distance to an unrelated center.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A radius 10 circle with a chord 12 units long has half-chord 6, so center-to-chord distance is \(\sqrt{100-36}=8\). If P lies 26 units from the center on the ray through the chord midpoint, beyond the chord, P’s perpendicular distance to the chord is \(26-8=18\); triangle PAB then has area \(\frac{12\cdot 18}{2}=108\). The center distance 26 is not its height.

activity.prompt: A rectangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 13. One rectangle side is 10. What is its area?
activity.explanation: The rectangle diagonal is the diameter 26. Its other side is \(\sqrt{26^{2}-10^{2}}=24\), giving area \(10\cdot 24=240\). Using the radius 13 as the diagonal would produce the wrong right triangle.

title: Distinguish one interior angle from exterior and total

section.heading: Distinguish one interior angle from exterior and total
body: An n-sided polygon has interior-angle sum \(\left(n-2\right) 180^\circ\). In a regular polygon the angles are equal, so each interior angle is \(\frac{180 \left(n-2\right)}{n}\) and each exterior angle is \(\frac{360}{n}\). One interior and its adjacent exterior add to \(180^\circ\). Equal exterior angles can therefore reveal n; the \(360^\circ\) exterior sum does not depend on the number of sides.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A regular 9-gon has total interior angle \(7\cdot 180=1260^\circ\) and each interior angle \(\frac{1260}{9}=140^\circ\). Its exterior angle is \(40^\circ\), confirming \(140+40=180^\circ\). If each exterior angle were \(24^\circ\), the regular polygon would have \(\frac{360}{24}=15\) sides, rather than 24 sides.

activity.prompt: A regular polygon has each exterior angle \(30^\circ\). How many sides does it have?
activity.explanation: The exterior angles make one full \(360^\circ\) turn. Thus \(n=\frac{360}{30}=12\). The interior angle is \(150^\circ\), which is a different quantity from the number of sides.

title: Subtract only the region actually removed

section.heading: Subtract only the region actually removed
body: Find the area of a composite region by adding its disjoint pieces or subtracting a removed area from the whole. A circle has area \(\pi  r^{2}\); a quarter-circle uses one fourth of that. The ring between concentric circles has area \(\pi  \left(R^{2}-r^{2}\right)\), not \(\pi  \left(R-r\right)^{2}\). Keep all lengths in one unit and check that subtracting a piece reduces the total.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A 12-by-5 rectangle with a radius 4 quarter-circle removed has area \(60-\frac{\pi  \left(4^{2}\right)}{4}=60-4 \pi\). For concentric radii 7 and 2, the ring area is \(\pi  \left(49-4\right)=45 \pi\). Squaring the radial width 5 instead would give \(25 \pi\) and describe a different circle rather than the ring.

activity.prompt: What is the area between concentric circles of radii 6 and 4?
activity.explanation: Subtract the areas: \(\pi \cdot 36-\pi \cdot 16=20 \pi\). The \(4 \pi\) choice squares only the radial difference 2, and \(40 \pi\) doubles the correct difference.

title: Use the base area before the perpendicular height

section.heading: Use the base area before the perpendicular height
body: A prism or cylinder has volume Bh, where B is its base area and h is perpendicular distance between bases. A pyramid or cone has one third of that volume, \(\frac{Bh}{3}\). A triangular base first needs \(\frac{bh}{2}\); a circular base needs \(\pi  r^{2}\). Do not substitute a slanted length for perpendicular height, and report cubic units.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A right triangular prism with base legs 5 and 12 and prism length 4 has base area 30 and volume 120. A cone with radius 6 and perpendicular height 5 has volume \(\frac{\pi \cdot 36\cdot 5}{3}=60 \pi\). The one-third factor distinguishes a cone from the corresponding cylinder; it does not replace the circular base-area formula.

activity.prompt: A cone has radius 2 and perpendicular height 9. What is its volume?
activity.explanation: Use \(\frac{\pi  r^{2} h}{3}=\frac{\pi \cdot 4\cdot 9}{3}=12 \pi\) cubic units. The \(36 \pi\) choice is the volume of a full cylinder with the same base and height.

title: Square the radius for a sphere’s surface area

section.heading: Square the radius for a sphere’s surface area
body: A sphere’s surface area is \(4 \pi  r^{2}\) and its volume is \(\frac{4 \pi  r^{3}}{3}\). Surface area measures its exposed two-dimensional boundary; volume measures the three-dimensional space inside. If a diameter is given, halve it before squaring. A cross-section through the center (a great circle) has area \(\pi  r^{2}\), which is one fourth of the sphere’s surface area.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For a sphere with diameter 10, the radius is 5. Surface area is \(4 \pi \cdot 25=100 \pi\) square units, while volume is \(\frac{500 \pi }{3}\) cubic units. Using 10 as the radius would quadruple the surface area because radius is squared.

activity.prompt: What is the surface area of a sphere with diameter 6?
activity.explanation: The radius is 3, so surface area is \(4 \pi \cdot 3^{2}=36 \pi\). The \(144 \pi\) choice uses the diameter as the radius; \(12 \pi\) does not square the radius correctly.

title: Use perpendicular heights for triangle and coordinate area

section.heading: Use perpendicular heights for triangle and coordinate area
body: For a triangle with a horizontal base, subtract x-coordinates for base length and use the vertical distance to its line as height. \(\text{Area}=\frac{bh}{2}\). For adjacent vectors(a, b), (c, d), a parallelogram has area \(\lvert ad-bc\rvert\) and the corresponding triangle has half that area. The determinant subtracts the slant contribution; multiplying vector magnitudes is valid only for perpendicular sides.

A triangle with known base b and perpendicular height h has area \(\frac{bh}{2}\) even without coordinates. A parallelogram instead has area bh. A slanted side is not substituted for the perpendicular height in either formula.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A triangle with vertices(−3, 2), (5, 2), (1, 8) has horizontal base 8 and height 6, so its area 24. Vectors(4, 1), (−2, 3) span a parallelogram of area \(\lvert 4\cdot 3-1 \left(-2\right)\rvert =14\). The associated triangle would have area 7; label which shape is requested.

activity.prompt: What is the area of the triangle with vertices(0, 1), (10, 1), (4, 7)?
activity.explanation: The base is 10 and the perpendicular height is \(7-1=6\). Triangle area is \(\frac{10\cdot 6}{2}=30\). The 60 choice omits the triangle’s half factor.

title: Complete both squares to identify a circle

section.heading: Complete both squares to identify a circle
body: A circle in standard form is \(\left(x-h\right)^{2}+\left(y-k\right)^{2}=r^{2}\), with center(h, k) and positive radius r. For a general equation with equal \(x^{2}\) and \(y^{2}\) coefficients, complete the square in each coordinate and balance the added constants. The signs inside the squares are opposite the center coordinates. The right side is radius squared, not radius.

The completing-square identity is \(x^{2}+px=\left(x+\frac{p}{2}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)^{2}\). Apply it independently to x and y, balancing both added constants before taking the positive square root for the radius.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: The equation \(x^{2}+y^{2}-8 x+6 y+9=0\) becomes \(\left(x-4\right)^{2}+\left(y+3\right)^{2}=16\). Add 16 and 9 to complete the two squares, leaving \(-9+16+9=16\) on the right. The center is(4, −3) and radius 4. Substitute(8, −3) to verify a point on the circle.

activity.prompt: What is the radius of \(\left(x+2\right)^{2}+\left(y-1\right)^{2}=49\)?
activity.explanation: The equation gives \(r^{2}=49\), so the positive radius is 7. The coordinates(−2, 1) specify the center and do not change the radius.

title: Recover an endpoint from a known midpoint

section.heading: Recover an endpoint from a known midpoint
body: A segment midpoint averages endpoint coordinates: \(M=\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}}{2},\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}\right)\). If M and one endpoint A are known, solve the averages to obtain \(B=2 M-A\) component by component. Averaging A and M again finds a quarter-point of the original segment, not the missing endpoint. Use parentheses around negative coordinates.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(A=\left(-5,6\right)\) and midpoint \(M=\left(3,1\right)\), then \(B=\left(2\cdot 3-\left(-5\right),2\cdot 1-6\right)=\left(11,-4\right)\). Checking the average of A and B gives \(\left(\frac{-5+11}{2},\frac{6-4}{2}\right)=\left(3,1\right)\), recovering the stated midpoint.

activity.prompt: A segment has endpoint(2, −3) and midpoint(5, 1). What is the other endpoint?
activity.explanation: Twice the midpoint minus the endpoint gives \(\left(10-2,2-\left(-3\right)\right)=\left(8,5\right)\). Check that averaging(2, −3) and(8, 5) gives(5, 1).

title: Take the negative reciprocal, then use a point

section.heading: Take the negative reciprocal, then use a point
body: For nonvertical lines, parallel slopes are equal and perpendicular slopes multiply to−1. Thus a perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, not merely the reciprocal or sign reversal. A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line, whose slope is undefined. Given a point, write \(y-y_{0}=m \left(x-x_{0}\right)\) to obtain the actual line equation.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A line with slope \(\frac{-2}{5}\) has perpendicular slope \(\frac{5}{2}\) because their product is−1. Through(1, 4), that perpendicular line has equation \(y-4=\left(\frac{5}{2}\right) \left(x-1\right)\). A vertical line \(x=3\) is perpendicular to any horizontal line \(y=c\); forcing a reciprocal formula with undefined slope is unnecessary.

activity.prompt: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to a line of slope \(\frac{7}{3}\)?
activity.explanation: The negative reciprocal of \(\frac{7}{3}\) is \(\frac{-3}{7}\). Its product with \(\frac{7}{3}\) is−1. Merely reversing the fraction gives the wrong sign; merely negating keeps the wrong magnitude.

title: Use the altitude of an equilateral triangle

section.heading: Use the altitude of an equilateral triangle
body: An equilateral triangle’s altitude bisects its base and forms two 30–60–90 triangles. With side s, the altitude is \(\frac{s \sqrt{3}}{2}\) and the area is \(\frac{s^{2} \sqrt{3}}{4}\). The side itself is not a perpendicular height. Its circumradius and inradius differ, so use only the length actually supplied before applying an area formula.

A regular hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles with side equal to the hexagon’s side. A side 2 therefore gives six areas \(\sqrt{3}\) and total \(6 \sqrt{3}\). More generally, a regular polygon’s area is half its perimeter times its perpendicular apothem.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For side 12, the altitude splits the base into lengths 6 and 6. Pythagoras gives height \(\sqrt{144-36}=6 \sqrt{3}\), so area \(\frac{12\cdot 6 \sqrt{3}}{2}=36 \sqrt{3}\). This also follows directly from \(\frac{12^{2} \sqrt{3}}{4}\).

activity.prompt: What is the area of an equilateral triangle of side 4?
activity.explanation: Use \(\frac{s^{2} \sqrt{3}}{4}=\frac{16 \sqrt{3}}{4}=4 \sqrt{3}\). The \(8 \sqrt{3}\) choice omits the triangle’s half factor after computing the altitude.

title: Match the side ratios adjacent to an angle bisector

section.heading: Match the side ratios adjacent to an angle bisector
body: If the bisector of angle A meets the opposite side BC at D, then \(\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}\). The two base pieces add to the whole BC. Reduce the side ratio, add its parts, and assign the base pieces in the same order. An angle bisector is not generally a median; equal base pieces require equal adjacent sides.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(AB=10\), \(AC=15\) and \(BC=20\), the bisector gives \(BD:DC=2:3\). Five parts make 20, so each part is 4. Therefore \(BD=8\) and \(DC=12\). Check \(8+12=20\) and \(\frac{8}{12}=\frac{10}{15}\) before choosing the requested segment.

activity.prompt: \(AB=6\), \(AC=9\), and \(BC=10\). The angle bisector from A meets BC at D. What is BD?
activity.explanation: The ratio BD: DC is \(6:9=2:3\). Thus BD is \(\frac{2}{5}\) of 10, giving 4. The 6 choice is DC; 5 assumes equal base pieces. The given sides 6, 9, 10 satisfy the triangle inequality.

title: Exclude degenerate endpoint lengths

section.heading: Exclude degenerate endpoint lengths
body: For positive sides a, b and third side x, a triangle exists exactly when \(\lvert a-b\rvert <x<a+b\). Both inequalities are strict: equality flattens the triangle into a straight segment. If x must be an integer, list the integers strictly inside the interval and count them, rather than rounding an endpoint into the allowed set.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: With sides 7 and 12, the third side must satisfy \(5<x<19\). Integer values 6 through 18 give 13 possibilities. A length 5 or 19 meets a non-strict bound but makes a degenerate triangle; neither is permitted.

activity.prompt: How many integer third-side lengths are possible when the other sides are 3 and 8?
activity.explanation: The strict interval is \(5<x<11\). Its integer values are 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, exactly five. Counting either endpoint would admit a flat triangle.

title: Translate to the rotation center before turning

section.heading: Translate to the rotation center before turning
body: About the origin, \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise maps(x, y) to(−y, x), \(90^\circ\) clockwise maps it to(y, −x), and \(180^\circ\) maps it to(−x, −y). For another center C, subtract C to form a displacement, apply the rotation, then add C back. This preserves the point’s distance from C; rotating the original coordinates directly uses the wrong center.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Rotate \(P=\left(5,1\right) 90^\circ\) counterclockwise about \(C=\left(2,-1\right)\). The displacement is(3, 2), which turns to(−2, 3). Adding the center gives(0, 2). The old and new displacements both have squared length 13, providing a quick geometric check.

activity.prompt: Rotate \(\left(3,2\right) 90^\circ\) counterclockwise about(1, 1). What is the image?
activity.explanation: The displacement from the center is(2, 1). It turns to(−1, 2); adding(1, 1) gives(0, 3). The other options rotate about the origin or in the wrong direction.

title: Use slant height for a cone’s exposed curved area

section.heading: Use slant height for a cone’s exposed curved area
body: A right circular cone has slant height \(\ell =\sqrt{r^{2}+h^{2}}\), where h is perpendicular height. Curved surface area is \(\pi  r \ell\); a closed cone also includes the circular base \(\pi  r^{2}\). Thus total area is \(\pi  r \ell +\pi  r^{2}\). The vertical height goes into volume \(\frac{\pi  r^{2} h}{3}\), not directly into the curved surface formula.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For radius 6 and perpendicular height 8, slant height is 10. Curved area is \(60 \pi\) and the base is \(36 \pi\), giving total \(96 \pi\) square units. Using \(h=8\) in place of \(\ell =10\) would understate the curved area, while omitting the base gives only the lateral surface.

activity.prompt: What is the total surface area of a closed cone with radius 8 and perpendicular height 15?
activity.explanation: The slant height is \(\sqrt{64+225}=17\). The curved surface is \(136 \pi\) and the base adds \(64 \pi\), giving \(200 \pi\). The \(136 \pi\) choice omits the base, and \(184 \pi\) uses the perpendicular height instead of the slant height.

title: Count each opposite pair of rectangular faces

section.heading: Count each opposite pair of rectangular faces
body: A closed rectangular box with side lengths l, w, h has six faces: two each of areas lw, lh, wh. Add them to obtain total surface area 2(lw+lh+wh). Multiplying lwh gives volume, while adding only one of each face gives half the surface. Check whether an open face should be omitted before applying the closed-box formula.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For a3-by-4-by-5 closed box, the distinct face areas are 12, 15, 20. Each occurs twice, giving \(2 \left(12+15+20\right)=94\) square units. Its volume 60 cubic units is a different measure and cannot answer a surface-area question.

activity.prompt: What is the surface area of a closed 2-by-5-by-7 box?
activity.explanation: The opposite face pairs total \(2 \left(2\cdot 5+2\cdot 7+5\cdot 7\right)=2 \left(10+14+35\right)=118\). The 59 choice counts just three faces; 70 is volume.

title: Distinguish an incircle from a circumcircle

section.heading: Distinguish an incircle from a circumcircle
body: The inradius r is triangle area divided by semiperimeter \(s=\frac{a+b+c}{2}\). In a right triangle, the circumradius R is half the hypotenuse because its midpoint is the circumcenter. Use Pythagoras to recover a missing hypotenuse. Keep the two radii distinct and form the requested ratio in the correct order.
For right-triangle legs a and b, area is \(\frac{ab}{2}\) and the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\). These supply all three side lengths and the area needed for \(r=\frac{A}{s}\).

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A right triangle with legs 8 and 15 has hypotenuse 17, area 60 and semiperimeter 20. Its inradius is \(\frac{60}{20}=3\) and circumradius \(\frac{17}{2}\). Thus \(\frac{r}{R}=\frac{6}{17}\). The centroid, where medians meet, is a different center and does not define either radius.

activity.prompt: A right triangle has legs 5 and 12. What is its inradius?
activity.explanation: The hypotenuse is 13, the area 30 and semiperimeter 15. Hence \(r=\frac{30}{15}=2\). The 6.5 choice is its circumradius, not the radius tangent to all three sides.

title: Locate the centroid along a median

section.heading: Locate the centroid along a median
body: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. The three medians meet at the centroid, which divides each median in a2: 1 ratio with the longer segment adjacent to the vertex. Thus vertex-to-centroid distance is \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the median. In coordinates, average all three vertices separately to find the centroid.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If a median has length 18, the centroid is 12 units from its vertex and 6 from the opposite midpoint. For vertices(0, 0), (9, 0), (0, 6), averaging gives centroid(3, 2). The median midpoint would instead divide its length 1: 1 and is generally not the centroid.

activity.prompt: A median has length 21. What is the vertex-to-centroid distance?
activity.explanation: The vertex is next to the longer 2-part segment. Two thirds of 21 is 14; 7 is the centroid-to-midpoint segment and 10.5 would bisect the median.

title: Choose the ratio from the named angle

section.heading: Choose the ratio from the named angle
body: In a right triangle, mark the acute angle first. \(\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), \(\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}\), and \(\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\). Recover a missing side with \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\) before changing ratios. For elevation, horizontal ground distance is adjacent and vertical rise is opposite; add eye height after finding the rise. To find an angle, use the matching inverse-trig operation in the correct angle mode.

Useful exact values are \(\sin 30^\circ =\frac{1}{2}\), \(\cos 30^\circ =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), \(\sin 45^\circ =\cos 45^\circ =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), \(\sin 60^\circ =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and \(\cos 60^\circ =\frac{1}{2}\). These follow from 30–60–90 and 45–45–90 triangles; use a calculator’s degree mode for other degree angles.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If an acute angle has sine \(\frac{8}{17}\), a reference triangle has opposite 8 and hypotenuse 17, so the adjacent side is 15 and tangent \(\frac{8}{15}\). A viewer 32 meters from a tower whose top rises 32 meters above eye level has tangent 1, hence elevation \(45^\circ\). With eye height 1.7 meters, total tower height is 33.7 meters.

activity.prompt: A ladder of length 14 makes \(30^\circ\) with level ground. How high does its top reach?
activity.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse and height is opposite the ground angle. Thus \(\text{height}=14 \sin 30^\circ =7\). Using cosine would find the horizontal distance \(7 \sqrt{3}\).

title: Recover a signed ratio before taking its reciprocal

section.heading: Recover a signed ratio before taking its reciprocal
body: On a reference triangle, use the given ratio to determine relative side lengths and a missing hypotenuse. Then assign signs from the quadrant: sine is positive in I, II; cosine in I, IV; tangent in I, III. \(\tan\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\). Cosecant, secant, cotangent are respectively the reciprocals of sine, cosine, tangent, wherever the denominator is nonzero.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If tangent is \(\frac{-8}{15}\) in Quadrant II, the reference hypotenuse is 17. Sine is \(\frac{8}{17}\), cosine \(\frac{-15}{17}\) and cotangent \(\frac{-15}{8}\). The positive sine and negative cosine produce the negative tangent; taking a reciprocal does not change its sign.

activity.prompt: If cosine is \(\frac{-7}{25}\) in Quadrant III, what is sine?
activity.explanation: The missing reference leg is \(\sqrt{25^{2}-7^{2}}=24\). Sine uses that leg over 25 and is negative in Quadrant III, so \(\frac{-24}{25}\). The \(\frac{-7}{24}\) choice uses the wrong pair of sides.

title: Build a double-angle identity from known ratios

section.heading: Build a double-angle identity from known ratios
body: Use \(\sin \left(2 \theta \right)=2 \sin \theta  \cos \theta\) and \(\cos \left(2 \theta \right)=1-2 \sin ^{2}\theta =2 \cos ^{2}\theta -1\). If tangent is supplied, reconstruct a reference triangle to obtain sine and cosine with quadrant signs first. Expanding \(\left(\sin \theta \pm \cos \theta \right)^{2}\) gives \(1\pm \sin \left(2 \theta \right)\), and the squared sum plus squared difference equals 2. Doubling an angle does not double a function value.

If \(\tan \theta =\frac{a}{b}\), choose reference legs \(\lvert a\rvert\) and \(\lvert b\rvert\), then hypotenuse \(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\). Divide the signed legs by that hypotenuse to recover sine and cosine before the identity; taking tangent as if it were sine uses the wrong denominator.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If sine is \(\frac{8}{17}\) in Quadrant II, cosine is \(\frac{-15}{17}\). Thus \(\sin \left(2 \theta \right)=\frac{-240}{289}\) and \(\cos \left(2 \theta \right)=\frac{225-64}{289}=\frac{161}{289}\). Separately, if \(\sin \theta -\cos \theta =\frac{2}{5}\), its square is \(\frac{4}{25}\); therefore \(\left(\sin \theta +\cos \theta \right)^{2}=2-\frac{4}{25}=\frac{46}{25}\) without solving for \(\theta\).

activity.prompt: If sine is \(\frac{5}{13}\), what is \(\cos \left(2 \theta \right)\)?
activity.explanation: Use \(1-2 \sin ^{2}\theta =1-\frac{50}{169}=\frac{119}{169}\). The \(\frac{120}{169}\) choice resembles a sine double-angle result, while \(\frac{25}{169}\) is only the squared original sine.

title: Rewrite equivalent trig expressions with restrictions

section.heading: Rewrite equivalent trig expressions with restrictions
body: The Pythagorean identity \(\sin ^{2}\theta +\cos ^{2}\theta =1\) lets you replace \(1-\sin ^{2}\theta\) with \(\cos ^{2}\theta\) and \(1-\cos ^{2}\theta\) with \(\sin ^{2}\theta\). Cancel factors only when the original denominator is nonzero. The cofunction identity \(\sin \left(\frac{\pi }{2}-\theta \right)=\cos \theta\) exchanges the ratios of complementary acute angles. Preserve sign information when taking a square root of a squared ratio.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\cos \theta \ne 0\), \(\frac{1-\sin ^{2}\theta }{\cos \theta }\) becomes \(\frac{\cos ^{2}\theta }{\cos \theta }=\cos \theta\). If \(\theta\) is acute and sine \(\frac{7}{25}\), cosine is \(\frac{24}{25}\), so \(\sin \left(\frac{\pi }{2}-\theta \right)=\frac{24}{25}\). Neither identity permits replacing \(\sin ^{2}\theta\) with \(\sin \left(\theta ^{2}\right)\) or splitting a square root across a subtraction.

activity.prompt: For \(\sin \theta \ne 0\), what equals \(\frac{1-\cos ^{2}\theta }{\sin ^{2}\theta }\)?
activity.explanation: The numerator equals \(\sin ^{2}\theta\). Dividing by the same nonzero square gives 1. The original \(\sin \theta \ne 0\) restriction remains; canceling only one factor would produce the wrong sine expression.

title: Use radians consistently in an arc calculation

section.heading: Use radians consistently in an arc calculation
body: A full turn is \(360^\circ\) or \(2 \pi\) radians. Convert degrees to radians with \(\frac{\pi }{180}\) and radians to degrees with \(\frac{180}{\pi }\). If \(\theta\) is already in radians, arc length is \(r \theta\); a degree angle instead uses the fraction \(\frac{\theta }{360}\) of circumference \(2 \pi  r\). Sector area is \(\frac{r^{2} \theta }{2}\) in radians. Check whether the answer is a distance, area, or angle.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: An angle \(120^\circ\) is \(\frac{120 \pi }{180}=\frac{2 \pi }{3}\) radians. On radius 9, its arc length is \(\frac{9\cdot 2 \pi }{3}=6 \pi\) and its sector area is \(\frac{\frac{81\cdot 2 \pi }{3}}{2}=27 \pi\). These use the same angle but different dimensions; converting a radian angle a second time would introduce an extra factor.

activity.prompt: What is the arc length for radius 5 and angle \(\frac{3 \pi }{5}\) radians?
activity.explanation: The angle is already in radians, so \(s=r \theta =\frac{5\cdot 3 \pi }{5}=3 \pi\). Do not multiply by another circumference factor or convert again.

title: Use a reference angle and coordinate signs

section.heading: Use a reference angle and coordinate signs
body: Unit-circle coordinates are \(\left(\cos \theta ,\sin \theta \right)\). At reference angles \(0^\circ\), \(30^\circ\), \(45^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), \(90^\circ\), sine is 0, \(\frac{1}{2}\), \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\), \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), 1 and cosine reverses that list. Locate the quadrant before applying the sign. Negative angles rotate clockwise: sine is odd and cosine is even. A reference angle measures the acute distance to the horizontal axis, not the entire rotation.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: At \(\frac{7 \pi }{4}=315^\circ\), the reference angle is \(\frac{\pi }{4}\) in Quadrant IV. Thus cosine is \(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\) and sine \(\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{2}\). A point \(\left(\frac{-1}{2},\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\) is in Quadrant III with reference \(60^\circ\), so its angle between \(0^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\) is \(240^\circ\).

activity.prompt: What is \(\cos \left(\frac{4 \pi }{3}\right)\)?
activity.explanation: The angle \(240^\circ\) lies in Quadrant III and has reference \(60^\circ\). Cosine has magnitude \(\frac{1}{2}\) and is negative there. The \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) magnitude belongs to sine at this reference angle.

title: Read amplitude, period, shift, and level crossings

section.heading: Read amplitude, period, shift, and level crossings
body: For \(y=A \sin \left(Bx+C\right)+D\) or its cosine version, \(\text{amplitude}=\lvert A\rvert\), \(\text{midline}=D\), \(\text{range}=\left[D-\lvert A\rvert ,D+\lvert A\rvert \right]\), and least positive \(\text{period}=\frac{2 \pi }{\lvert B\rvert }\) for nonzero A, B. Tangent has period \(\frac{\pi }{\lvert B\rvert }\). Factor the inside to find shift \(\frac{-C}{B}\). To solve a level crossing, first recover these parameters, isolate the trig ratio, then divide the matching inner angle by B.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(y=4 \cos \left(2 x-\frac{\pi }{2}\right)+3\), amplitude 4, range[−1, 7], period \(\pi\) and shift \(\frac{\pi }{4}\) right. Conversely, an unshifted \(y=A \cos \left(Bx\right)+D\) with A, \(B>0\) and maximum 9, minimum 1 and period \(\pi\) has \(A=4\), \(D=5\), \(B=2\). To reach \(y=3\), solve \(\cos \left(2 x\right)=\frac{-1}{2}\); the first positive solution is \(x=\frac{\pi }{3}\).

activity.prompt: For \(y=5 \sin \left(3 x-\pi \right)\), what is its horizontal shift?
activity.explanation: Factor \(3 x-\pi =3 \left(x-\frac{\pi }{3}\right)\), giving a right shift \(\frac{\pi }{3}\). The input coefficient divides the phase constant; the outside amplitude 5 does not determine horizontal movement.

title: Use the included angle when a triangle is not right

section.heading: Use the included angle when a triangle is not right
body: With two known sides a, b and their included angle C, the opposite side satisfies \(c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2 ab \cos C\). Pair the requested side with its opposite angle. For obtuse C, cosine is negative, so the final subtraction increases \(c^{2}\). Take the positive square root for a length; the Pythagorean theorem alone assumes a right angle.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Sides 3 and 8 enclosing \(120^\circ\) give \(c^{2}=9+64-48 \left(\frac{-1}{2}\right)=97\), so \(c=\sqrt{97}\). The right-angle counterpart would be \(\sqrt{73}\), smaller as expected. The side remains less than \(3+8=11\), satisfying the triangle inequality.

activity.prompt: Sides 6 and 7 enclose \(60^\circ\). What is the opposite side length?
activity.explanation: Compute \(c^{2}=36+49-84 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=43\), so \(c=\sqrt{43}\). The \(\sqrt{85}\) choice omits the cosine term and assumes a right angle; 13 is the sum of the sides, a degenerate limit.

title: Pair opposite sides and check the second sine branch

section.heading: Pair opposite sides and check the second sine branch
body: The law of sines is \(\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}\). Pair each side with the angle directly opposite it. If two sides and a nonincluded angle are known, solving for a sine may yield both B and \(180^\circ -B\). Test each branch against \(A+B<180^\circ\) and a positive third angle; the data can produce zero, one, or two triangles.
If the computed sine of a proposed angle exceeds 1, no real angle and therefore no triangle fits. If a branch makes the third angle zero or negative, reject it even if the sine value itself is valid.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(A=45^\circ\), \(B=60^\circ\) and \(a=8 \sqrt{2}\), then \(b=\frac{a \sin 60^\circ }{\sin 45^\circ }=8 \sqrt{3}\). In an SSA case \(A=30^\circ\), \(a=9\), \(b=12\), sine law gives \(\sin B=\frac{2}{3}\). Both \(B\approx 41.81^\circ\) and \(B\approx 138.19^\circ\) leave a positive third angle, so two different triangles fit.

activity.prompt: If \(A=30^\circ\), \(B=60^\circ\) and side \(a=7\), what is side b?
activity.explanation: Sine law gives \(b=\frac{7 \sin 60^\circ }{\sin 30^\circ }=7 \sqrt{3}\). The larger angle has the larger opposite side, confirming \(b>7\). Reversing the sine ratio gives \(\frac{7}{\sqrt{3}}\).

title: Use the sine to supply a perpendicular height

section.heading: Use the sine to supply a perpendicular height
body: If sides a, b enclose angle C, triangle area is \(\frac{ab \sin C}{2}\). The factor sin C turns side b into a perpendicular height relative to side a. The angle must be the included angle; an angle opposite a different side cannot be substituted without more work. Both the triangle half factor and the sine factor are needed.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Sides 9 and 12 enclosing \(30^\circ\) give area \(\frac{9\cdot 12\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2}=27\). A rectangle using the two side lengths would have area 108, and a triangle using 12 as an assumed perpendicular height would give 54. The sine factor is what corrects the slanted side.

activity.prompt: Two sides are 5 and 16 with included angle \(30^\circ\). What is the triangle area?
activity.explanation: \(\text{Area}=\frac{5\cdot 16\cdot \sin 30^\circ }{2}=\frac{80\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2}=20\). The 40 choice drops one of the half factors, and 80 drops both.

title: List every periodic solution in the allowed interval

section.heading: List every periodic solution in the allowed interval
body: An inverse-trig button gives a principal value, not the complete solution set. Isolate the trig ratio, identify all matching angles, and add whole periods that keep the inner angle in range. For sin(Bx) or cos(Bx), map the original x interval into a Bx interval before counting, then divide back. Include or exclude endpoints exactly as stated.

For a quadratic trig equation, first set \(u=\sin \theta\) or \(\cos \theta\) and solve the polynomial in u. Reject ratios outside[−1, 1], then list all angles for every surviving ratio. For \(2 \cos ^{2}\theta +\cos \theta -1=0\), factoring gives \(\cos \theta =\frac{1}{2}\) or−1, with three solutions \(\frac{\pi }{3}\), \(\pi\), \(\frac{5 \pi }{3}\) on one full turn.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\sin \left(2 x\right)=\frac{1}{2}\) on \(0\le x<2 \pi\), the inner angle spans \(0\le 2 x<4 \pi\). Its solutions are \(\frac{\pi }{6}\), \(\frac{5 \pi }{6}\), \(\frac{13 \pi }{6}\), \(\frac{17 \pi }{6}\), so \(x=\frac{\pi }{12}\), \(\frac{5 \pi }{12}\), \(\frac{13 \pi }{12}\), \(\frac{17 \pi }{12}\). A single arcsine value would miss three valid answers.

activity.prompt: How many zeros does sin(3 x) have for \(0\le x<2 \pi\)?
activity.explanation: Zeros satisfy \(3 x=k \pi\), or \(x=\frac{k \pi }{3}\). In the interval, \(k=0\), 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 gives six zeros. The next \(k=6\) corresponds to the excluded upper endpoint \(2 \pi\).

title: Rebuild totals before averaging

section.heading: Rebuild totals before averaging
body: \(\text{mean}=\frac{\text{total}}{\text{count}}\). To combine groups, multiply each mean by its count, add the totals, and divide by the combined count. Adding or removing observations changes both the total and the count. If every observation becomes ax+b, the mean becomes \(a \mu +b\). An unweighted average of group means works only for equal-size groups.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Six scores average 14, so they total 84. Removing a score 9 leaves 75 across five scores, giving mean 15. If another four scores average 20, combining all original ten gives \(\frac{84+80}{10}=16.4\). If every combined score is increased by 3, its new mean is 19.4; the same constant shifts every observation and the mean.

activity.prompt: Four values average 18. A fifth value 28 is added. What is the new mean?
activity.explanation: The first four total 72. Adding 28 gives 100 over five observations, so the mean is 20. Averaging 18 and 28 equally gives 23 but treats the four-value group as one observation.

title: Relocate the middle after changing a data set

section.heading: Relocate the middle after changing a data set
body: Sort observations before finding a median. An odd count has one central value; an even count uses the average of the two central values. Adding an observation changes the central positions even if the old values are unchanged. An extreme outlier can move the mean substantially while leaving the median fixed; calculate each statistic from its own definition.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, the median is 8. Adding 100 produces six values with central 8 and 11, so the new median is 9.5. If instead five copies of 7 receive an added 100, both central values remain 7, while the new mean is \(\frac{135}{6}=22.5\). A median resists an outlier but is not guaranteed to stay unchanged.

activity.prompt: The sorted data are 1, 4, 9, 12. After adding 20, what is the median?
activity.explanation: The new list has five observations, so its middle is the third value 9. The old median was \(\frac{4+9}{2}=6.5\); neither an unsorted position nor the average of arbitrary middle-looking values is the new median.

title: Calculate and transform variance and standard deviation
