section.heading: Calculate and transform variance and standard deviation
body: Population variance is the mean of squared distances from the population mean; standard deviation is its square root. A sample variance instead divides the sum by n−1. Under \(y=ax+b\), standard deviation multiplies by \(\lvert a\rvert\) and variance by \(a^{2}\); adding b changes neither spread. Two data sets differing by a constant therefore have equal standard deviations.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: The population 2, 6, 10 has mean 6 and squared deviations 16, 0, 16, giving variance \(\frac{32}{3}\) and standard deviation \(\sqrt{\frac{32}{3}}\). Under \(y=-3 x+5\), variance becomes \(\frac{9\cdot 32}{3}=96\) and standard deviation becomes \(3 \sqrt{\frac{32}{3}}\). The reflection does not make standard deviation negative, and the shift 5 does not enter either spread calculation.

activity.prompt: A data set has standard deviation 4. Every value becomes−5 x+12. What is the new standard deviation?
activity.explanation: Standard deviation scales by the absolute multiplier 5, giving 20. A negative scale reflects the values but spread remains nonnegative; adding 12 shifts the center without increasing spread.

title: Use frequencies as counts, including an unknown count

section.heading: Use frequencies as counts, including an unknown count
body: A frequency table repeats each displayed value as many times as its count states. \(\text{mean}=\frac{\sum (\text{value}\cdot\text{frequency})}{\sum\text{frequency}}\); a fraction below a cutoff adds only frequencies meeting the condition. For an unknown frequency, set this mean expression equal to the given mean and solve. Two same-score people can be counted within each group using \(C \left(n,2\right)=\frac{n \left(n-1\right)}{2}\), divided by that count for the whole sample.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A table has k scores 1, two scores 3 and two scores 7, with mean 3. The equation \(\frac{k+20}{k+4}=3\) gives \(k=4\), so there are 8 observations. If two people are chosen without replacement, equal-score pairs total \(C \left(4,2\right)+C \left(2,2\right)+C \left(2,2\right)=8\) out of \(C \left(8,2\right)=28\), giving \(\frac{2}{7}\). Counts, not distinct score labels, define the sample space.

activity.prompt: A table lists 10 three times, 20 twice, and 40 once. What is its mean?
activity.explanation: The total is \(10\cdot 3+20\cdot 2+40=110\) over six observations, giving \(\frac{110}{6}=\frac{55}{3}\). The \(\frac{70}{3}\) choice averages only the distinct labels; 110 is the total rather than the mean.

title: Define the sample space before counting favorable outcomes

section.heading: Define the sample space before counting favorable outcomes
body: For equally likely outcomes, \(P=\frac{\text{favorable outcomes}}{\text{total outcomes}}\). Two labeled dice give 36 ordered pairs; their possible sums are not equally likely. For selecting two distinct objects without order from n, total pairs are \(C \left(n,2\right)=\frac{n \left(n-1\right)}{2}\). A sum is odd exactly when one term is odd and the other even; count all such pairs without counting either order twice.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Two fair dice sum to 10 in(4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 4), so the chance is \(\frac{3}{36}=\frac{1}{12}\). For two cards chosen from 1 through 8, four are odd and four even, producing 16 odd-sum pairs among \(C \left(8,2\right)=28\), so the probability is \(\frac{4}{7}\). The sum-based outcomes are not uniformly distributed.

activity.prompt: When two fair dice are rolled, what is the probability their sum is 11?
activity.explanation: The favorable ordered pairs are(5, 6)and(6, 5), two of 36 equally likely pairs. Thus \(\frac{2}{36}=\frac{1}{18}\). Dividing by the number of possible sums incorrectly assumes equal sum probabilities.

title: Choose committees without assigning roles

section.heading: Choose committees without assigning roles
body: If order or roles do not matter, use \(C \left(n,k\right)=\frac{n!}{k! \left(n-k\right)!}\). Multiplying n(n−1)…counts ordered assignments and overcounts each k-person group k!times. If a group must include fixed numbers from different categories, choose from each category separately and multiply. Check that the categories do not overlap before treating the choices as separate.
The symbol n!means \(1\cdot 2\)·…\(· n\) for a positive integer n, and \(0!=1\). These factorials count arrangements; the denominator removes orderings of the same chosen group.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A committee requiring two of six writers and one of four editors can be chosen in \(C \left(6,2\right)\cdot C \left(4,1\right)=15\cdot 4=60\) ways. The writer pair has no first and second role, so \(6\cdot 5\) would count it twice. A four-person committee from ten people has \(C \left(10,4\right)=210\) possibilities.

activity.prompt: How many three-person committees can be chosen from seven people with no assigned roles?
activity.explanation: Use \(C \left(7,3\right)=\frac{7\cdot 6\cdot 5}{3\cdot 2\cdot 1}=35\). The 210 choice assigns an order to the three people, counting each committee six times.

title: Update the counts after an item is removed

section.heading: Update the counts after an item is removed
body: Without replacement, the second draw uses a smaller total and may use a smaller favorable count. Multiply along a specified order, then add mutually exclusive valid orders. If an earlier removed item is already known, start from the updated bag; do not multiply by the probability of that known event. Replacement instead restores the original counts.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A bag has 4 red and 3 blue tokens. Red then blue has probability \(\left(\frac{4}{7}\right) \left(\frac{3}{6}\right)=\frac{2}{7}\); blue then red also has \(\frac{2}{7}\), so different colors have \(\frac{4}{7}\). If one blue is already removed, the next-red probability is \(\frac{4}{6}=\frac{2}{3}\): the known removal is a condition, not another random event to multiply.

activity.prompt: A bag has 5 red and 2 blue tokens. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
activity.explanation: The first-red probability is \(\frac{5}{7}\). After that red is removed, the next-red probability is \(\frac{4}{6}\). Multiply to obtain \(\frac{20}{42}=\frac{10}{21}\). The \(\frac{25}{49}\) choice incorrectly models replacement.

title: Weight signed net outcomes by their probabilities

section.heading: Weight signed net outcomes by their probabilities
body: Expected value is the probability-weighted mean: sum each outcome times its probability. Use a negative value for a loss. If the listed outcomes are payouts before an entry cost, subtract that cost once; if they are already net gains, do not subtract again. When colors determine a payout, first derive each event probability from updated draws or unordered pair counts \(C \left(n,2\right)=\frac{n \left(n-1\right)}{2}\).

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A game paying 10 with probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) and 0 otherwise, with a2 entry cost, has expected net gain \(\frac{10}{3}-2=\frac{4}{3}\). In a bag with 5 red and 3 blue, matching-color unordered pairs number \(C \left(5,2\right)+C \left(3,2\right)=13\) out of \(C \left(8,2\right)=28\). If matching pays 4 and a game costs 1, expected net gain is \(\frac{4\cdot 13}{28}-1=\frac{6}{7}\).

activity.prompt: A game pays 9 with probability 0.4 and 0 otherwise. It costs 2 to enter. What is the expected net gain?
activity.explanation: Expected payout is \(9\cdot 0.4=3.60\). Subtract the certain 2 entry cost to obtain 1.60. Equivalently, net outcomes 7 and−2 give \(7 \left(0.4\right)-2 \left(0.6\right)=1.60\).

title: Restrict the denominator to the stated group

section.heading: Restrict the denominator to the stated group
body: Conditional probability \(P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}\), with \(P \left(B\right)>0\). Read given B as among B: count only the eligible row, column, or subgroup. Reversing the condition usually changes the denominator. The full population can supply table context without belonging in the requested fraction.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Among 30 musicians, 18 sing; among 20 nonmusicians, 6 sing. If a singer is selected, 18 of the 24 eligible singers are musicians, giving \(\frac{3}{4}\). Selecting a musician instead would give singer probability \(\frac{18}{30}=\frac{3}{5}\). These are different questions even though the same overlap 18 appears.

activity.prompt: A club has 15 runners, of whom 6 also cycle. There are 20 cyclists total. Among cyclists, what fraction run?
activity.explanation: The condition limits selection to 20 cyclists. Six are also runners, so the probability is \(\frac{6}{20}=\frac{3}{10}\). The \(\frac{6}{15}\) choice reverses the condition and selects among runners.

title: Test independence separately from being disjoint

section.heading: Test independence separately from being disjoint
body: Events A and B are independent when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\): learning that one happened does not change the chance of the other. Disjoint events have \(P(A\cap B)=0\) and cannot occur together. With both marginal probabilities positive, disjoint events cannot also be independent. Compare the stated intersection to both zero and the product rather than treating the words as synonyms.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(P \left(A\right)=0.5\), \(P \left(B\right)=0.6\) and intersection 0.3, the product matches 0.3, so the events are independent. Their intersection is positive, so they are not disjoint. For a separate example, let \(P(A)=0.2\), \(P(B)=0.5\), and \(P(A\cap B)=0\). These events are disjoint but dependent because \(0\ne 0.2\cdot 0.5\). Their union is 0.7, a valid probability.

activity.prompt: \(P \left(A\right)=0.2\), \(P \left(B\right)=0.5\), and \(P(A\cap B)=0.1\). Which description is correct?
activity.explanation: The product \(0.2\cdot 0.5=0.1\) matches the stated intersection, establishing independence. Since that intersection is nonzero, the events can occur together and are not disjoint.

title: Subtract the overlap once for an inclusive or

section.heading: Subtract the overlap once for an inclusive or
body: An inclusive A or B includes outcomes in either event or both. Its probability is P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). The subtraction removes the double count of shared outcomes. For integer divisibility, numbers divisible by both a and b are multiples of their least common multiple; count only within the stated inclusive range.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Among integers 1 through 24, eight are multiples of 3 and six are multiples of 4. Two multiples of 12 are in both groups. Thus a multiple of 3 or 4 occurs in \(8+6-2=12\) of 24 outcomes, probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). Counting 14 would double-count 12 and 24.

activity.prompt: If \(P \left(A\right)=0.6\), \(P \left(B\right)=0.5\), and their overlap is 0.3, what is P(A or B)?
activity.explanation: Add the individual probabilities and subtract the shared portion: \(0.6+0.5-0.3=0.8\). A probability greater than 1 signals double-counted outcomes or another invalid setup.

title: Calculate at least one by subtracting none

section.heading: Calculate at least one by subtracting none
body: The complement of at least one success is no successes. For independent trials with success probability p, n failures have probability \(\left(1-p\right)^{n}\), so at least one success is \(1-\left(1-p\right)^{n}\). Adding individual success probabilities can double-count multiple successes. Verify independence or update conditional probabilities before multiplying failure chances.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For five independent trials with success probability 0.2, no success has probability \(0.8^{5}=0.32768\). Therefore at least one success has probability 0.67232. For two fair dice, at least one 1 equals \(1-\left(\frac{5}{6}\right)^{2}=\frac{11}{36}\); simply adding \(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}\) counts the double-one outcome twice.

activity.prompt: Four independent trials each succeed with probability \(\frac{1}{2}\). What is the probability of at least one success?
activity.explanation: All four fail with probability \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4}=\frac{1}{16}\). Subtract from 1 to get \(\frac{15}{16}\). The \(\frac{1}{16}\) choice is the complement, not the requested event.

title: Count placements of exactly k successes

section.heading: Count placements of exactly k successes
body: For n independent trials with the same success chance p, exactly k successes has probability \(C \left(n,k\right) p^{k} \left(1-p\right)^{n-k}\). A specific success/failure order has the product part; C(n, k)counts the different placements of those successes. The word exactly excludes outcomes with more successes. A fair coin supplies \(p=\frac{1}{2}\).

For at least k successes, add the mutually exclusive counts k, k+1, …, n. For example, at least 3 heads in four fair tosses combines exactly 3 and exactly 4; the different-count events do not overlap.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Exactly two successes in five trials with \(p=0.4\) has \(C \left(5,2\right)=10\) possible placements. Each placement has probability \(0.4^{2}\cdot 0.6^{3}=0.03456\), so the total is 0.3456. Counting one ordering alone misses nine equally specified placements.

activity.prompt: What is the probability of exactly one head in four fair independent tosses?
activity.explanation: The single head can occupy any of four positions, each sequence having probability \(\frac{1}{16}\). Thus \(\frac{4}{16}=\frac{1}{4}\). This includes H T T T and the other three placements, not every outcome with a head.

title: Keep the required order for a first-success trial

section.heading: Keep the required order for a first-success trial
body: First success on trial n means exactly n−1 failures followed by one success in that order. With independent equal-chance trials, the probability is \(\left(1-p\right)^{n-1} p\). Do not multiply by a combination count: placing the success earlier would violate the first-success condition. This differs from exactly one success anywhere among n trials.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If each attempt succeeds with probability 0.3, first success on attempt 4 requires F, F, F, S, with probability \(0.7^{3}\cdot 0.3=0.1029\). Exactly one success among four attempts would also include S, F, F, F and two other positions, giving a different event.

activity.prompt: Each independent trial succeeds with probability \(\frac{1}{4}\). What is the probability the first success occurs on trial 2?
activity.explanation: Trial 1 must fail and trial 2 must succeed, so multiply \(\left(\frac{3}{4}\right) \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{3}{16}\). The \(\frac{1}{16}\) choice describes two successes; \(\frac{1}{4}\) omits the required first failure.

title: Assign positions without allowing repeats

section.heading: Assign positions without allowing repeats
body: When positions or roles are distinct, multiply the eligible choices at each step. For r positions chosen from n different objects without repeats, the count is n(n−1)…\(\left(n-r+1\right)=\frac{n!}{\left(n-r\right)!}\). If repeats are allowed, each position may retain n choices. An unordered group instead requires dividing out its r!orderings.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A four-character code using different letters from seven has \(7\cdot 6\cdot 5\cdot 4=840\) possibilities. A seven-letter alphabet with repeats allowed would give \(7^{4}=2401\). Merely choosing an unordered four-letter group gives \(C \left(7,4\right)=35\) and loses the order needed for a code.

activity.prompt: Three distinct prizes go to three of six people, with nobody winning twice. How many assignments are possible?
activity.explanation: The three different prizes create ordered positions. There are 6, 5, 4 eligible winners in succession, giving 120. The 20 choice counts unordered groups and 216 permits repeat winners.

title: Divide out swaps of indistinguishable objects

section.heading: Divide out swaps of indistinguishable objects
body: For n arranged objects with repeated groups of sizes \(r_{1}\), \(r_{2}\), …, the number of distinct arrangements is \(\frac{n!}{r_1!r_2!\cdots}\). Swapping two identical copies does not create a new arrangement, so each repeat-group factorial divides the labeled count. Use each object exactly as many times as it appears; this is different from allowing unrestricted repeats in a code.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: The word PEPPER has six letters with three Ps and two Es. Its distinct arrangements number \(\frac{6!}{3! 2!}=60\). Labeling the Ps separately would count each visible arrangement 3!times and labeling the Es would count another 2!times; dividing both removes those duplicate labels.

activity.prompt: How many distinct arrangements use all letters in MOM?
activity.explanation: There are three positions and two indistinguishable Ms, so \(\frac{3!}{2!}=3\). The visible arrangements are MOM, MMO, OMM. Counting six would distinguish the two identical Ms.

title: Separate sampling bias from treatment assignment

section.heading: Separate sampling bias from treatment assignment
body: Random sampling helps generalize from a sample to the population covered by its sampling frame. Volunteers may differ from nonvolunteers, and a larger volunteer sample does not remove that bias. Random assignment to treatment/control groups supports causal comparison within a sound experiment; it does not automatically make the subjects representative. Observational association alone does not establish causation.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If a school asks only students already attending tutoring whether tutoring is desirable, the sampling frame omits nonattenders and may overstate schoolwide interest. Randomly selecting from that attendee list still cannot represent students excluded from it. In a separate volunteer experiment, random treatment assignment can support a treatment comparison within the volunteers without proving a schoolwide effect.

activity.prompt: A large survey uses only responses from volunteers at a sports club. What is its main limitation for estimating all residents’ exercise habits?
choices: The sample may systematically differ from all residents
A large sample has no random error
Randomly choosing among these volunteers guarantees representation
activity.explanation: The volunteer sports-club frame can overrepresent active residents and excludes others. Random selection within that frame does not repair who was omitted; increasing its size does not remove the selection bias.

title: Measure the width of the middle half

section.heading: Measure the width of the middle half
body: The interquartile range is \(IQR=Q_{3}-Q_{1}\), where \(Q_{1}\) and \(Q_{3}\) bound the middle 50%of observations. It measures spread, not center. The full range instead needs maximum−minimum. Follow any quartile convention supplied by a question; if the quartiles are already given, subtract them directly rather than trying to reconstruct the data.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(Q_{1}=11\) and \(Q_{3}=27\), the IQR is 16. The midpoint of those quartiles is 19, which describes a different summary. An extreme maximum can change the full range without changing either quartile, so IQR can be less sensitive to an outlier.

activity.prompt: If \(Q_{1}=14\) and \(Q_{3}=35\), what is the IQR?
activity.explanation: The IQR is \(35-14=21\). Averaging the quartiles gives 24.5 and adding them gives 49; neither measures the width between them.

title: Express a distance from the mean in SD units

section.heading: Express a distance from the mean in SD units
body: The standardized distance \(z=\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma }\) subtracts the mean before dividing by the positive standard deviation. A value above the mean has positive z and a value below it has negative z. Standardization alone does not imply a normal distribution or assign a percentile; it simply changes the distance unit from raw-score points to standard deviations.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A measurement 44 in a population with mean 50 and standard deviation 3 has \(z=\frac{44-50}{3}=-2\). It lies two standard deviations below the mean. Dividing 44 by 3 would measure the score from zero, not from the mean; omitting the sign loses whether it is above or below.

activity.prompt: A score 91 comes from a distribution with mean 70 and standard deviation 7. How many standard deviations above the mean is it?
activity.explanation: Subtract 70 from 91 to obtain 21, then divide by 7 to get 3. The 21 choice is the raw-score distance and 13 is the raw score divided by the standard deviation.

title: Distribute complex products and replace i²

section.heading: Distribute complex products and replace i²
body: Treat real terms and multiples of i as different like-term groups, with \(i^{2}=-1\). Distribute every term in a complex product. In \(\left(a+bi\right)^{2}\), keep the middle term 2 abi; the square is \(a^{2}-b^{2}+2 abi\), not the squared magnitude \(a^{2}+b^{2}\). Combine the real and imaginary parts only after replacing powers of i.
For addition, combine real parts and imaginary coefficients directly: \(\left(1+4 i\right)+\left(3-2 i\right)=4+2 i\). No \(i^{2}\) appears unless an actual multiplication produces it.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: \(\left(2+3 i\right) \left(4-i\right)=8-2 i+12 i-3 i^{2}=11+10 i\). Also, \(\left(3-2 i\right)^{2}=9-12 i+4 i^{2}=5-12 i\). The real correction has a minus sign because \(i^{2}=-1\); an algebraic square can remain complex even though a magnitude is real.

activity.prompt: What is \(\left(1+2 i\right) \left(3-i\right)\)?
activity.explanation: Distribute to obtain \(3-i+6 i-2 i^{2}\). Since \(-2 i^{2}=2\), the result is \(5+5 i\). The \(1+5 i\) choice treats \(i^{2}\) as+1, while \(5-5i\) reverses the imaginary sign.

title: Multiply by the denominator’s conjugate

section.heading: Multiply by the denominator’s conjugate
body: The conjugate of a+bi is a−bi; their product is \(a^{2}+b^{2}\). Divide complex numbers by multiplying both numerator and denominator by the denominator’s conjugate, then distribute and replace \(i^{2}=-1\). A nonzero complex denominator has a positive squared magnitude, making the new denominator real. Changing only the denominator would change the value.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\frac{5+i}{2-i}\), multiply by \(\frac{2+i}{2+i}\). The numerator is \(10+7 i+i^{2}=9+7 i\) and the denominator \(4-i^{2}=5\). Thus the quotient is \(\frac{9+7 i}{5}\). Using 2−i again would keep an imaginary denominator instead of rationalizing it.

activity.prompt: What is \(\frac{2+i}{1-i}\)?
activity.explanation: Multiply top and bottom by 1+i. The numerator is \(2+3 i+i^{2}=1+3 i\); the denominator is 2. Therefore the quotient is \(\frac{1+3 i}{2}\).

title: Measure a complex number’s distance from the origin

section.heading: Measure a complex number’s distance from the origin
body: For \(z=a+bi\), magnitude \(\lvert z\rvert =\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\), a nonnegative real number. Its square is \(a^{2}+b^{2}\), distinct from the algebraic square \(z^{2}\). Magnitudes multiply under complex multiplication and divide under division by a nonzero number. The signs of real and imaginary coordinates disappear inside the squares, but adding their absolute values measures a different path.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(z=-8+15 i\), magnitude is \(\sqrt{64+225}=17\), while \(\lvert z\rvert ^{2}=289\). If \(w=3-4 i\), then \(\lvert \frac{z}{w}\rvert =\frac{17}{5}\) without needing a full complex division. The sum \(8+15=23\) is the distance along two coordinate legs, not the straight distance.

activity.prompt: What is the magnitude of \(-7-24 i\)?
activity.explanation: Use \(\sqrt{\left(-7\right)^{2}+\left(-24\right)^{2}}=\sqrt{625}=25\). The 31 choice adds absolute coordinates; subtracting their magnitudes would give 17 instead of the Euclidean distance.

title: Complete component operations before taking a magnitude

section.heading: Complete component operations before taking a magnitude
body: Add or subtract vectors component by component and multiply every component by a scalar. The magnitude of(x, y)is \(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\). To make a unit vector in the same direction, divide each component by the vector’s positive magnitude; the zero vector has no direction to normalize. Magnitude is taken after forming the requested vector, not separately before an addition or subtraction.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(u=\left(3,-1\right)\), \(v=\left(-2,4\right)\), the vector \(2 u-v=\left(6,-2\right)-\left(-2,4\right)=\left(8,-6\right)\), whose magnitude is 10. Dividing by 10 gives unit direction \(\left(\frac{4}{5},\frac{-3}{5}\right)\). Subtracting the two original magnitudes would not equal the magnitude of 2 u−v.

activity.prompt: If \(u=\left(1,4\right)\) and \(v=\left(3,-2\right)\), what is \(\lvert u+v\rvert\)?
activity.explanation: The sum is(4, 2), so its magnitude is \(\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}\). Add components first; 6 is the sum of the component magnitudes, not the vector’s length.

title: Add component products to test perpendicularity

section.heading: Add component products to test perpendicularity
body: The dot product of \(\left(u_{1},u_{2}\right)\) and \(\left(v_{1},v_{2}\right)\) is the scalar \(u_{1} v_{1}+u_{2} v_{2}\). For nonzero vectors it also equals \(\lvert u\rvert  \lvert v\rvert  \cos \theta\). Perpendicular vectors therefore have dot product zero; a negative result corresponds to an obtuse angle, not a negative length. Solve a missing component by setting the complete dot product to zero rather than comparing component ratios.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(u=\left(2,-5\right)\), \(v=\left(4,3\right)\), the dot product is \(8-15=-7\). A vector(k, 4)perpendicular to(3, −6)must satisfy \(3 k-24=0\), giving \(k=8\). A componentwise product(8, −15)is not the dot product until its entries are added.

activity.prompt: What k makes(k, 5)perpendicular to(2, −4)?
activity.explanation: Perpendicularity requires \(2 k-20=0\), so \(k=10\). Taking a component ratio instead of the dot product tests a different relationship.

title: Check dimensions, then multiply a row by a column

section.heading: Check dimensions, then multiply a row by a column
body: If A is \(m\times n\) and B is \(n\times p\), AB exists and is \(m\times p\). Compute an entry by multiplying corresponding terms from a row of A and a column of B, then adding. Matrix multiplication is not entrywise multiplication and generally \(AB\ne BA\); BA may not exist. If asked for one entry, calculate only the named row and column while preserving order.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A \(2\times 3\) matrix times \(a 3\times 4\) matrix produces \(2\times 4\). For A with rows(1, 2), (3, 1)and B with columns(4, −1), (2, 5), the entry in row 2, column 1 of AB is \(3\cdot 4+1 \left(-1\right)=11\). Using row 1 would instead compute a different product entry.

activity.prompt: A is \(4\times 2\) and B is \(2\times 5\). What are the dimensions of AB?
activity.explanation: The inner dimensions 2 match, so multiplication is defined. The output uses the outer dimensions: 4 rows and 5 columns. The inner 2 does not set the result’s shape.

title: Prove a pattern using repeated matrix multiplication

section.heading: Prove a pattern using repeated matrix multiplication
body: A matrix power means repeated matrix multiplication, not powering each entry separately. For a matrix with rows(1, c), (0, 1), multiplying a same-shaped matrix with upper-right entry t by it gives upper-right t+c and leaves the diagonal 1 and lower-left 0. This establishes a linear entry pattern across powers; check the first product and the next product before generalizing.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Let A have rows(1, 3), (0, 1). \(A^{2}\) has rows(1, 6), (0, 1), and another multiplication gives \(A^{3}\) with upper-right 9. In general Aⁿhas upper-right 3 n. The sum of its four entries is \(2+3 n\). This rule follows from the actual row-column product, not from 3ⁿ.

activity.prompt: A has rows(1, 2), (0, 1). What is the upper-right entry of \(A^{4}\)?
activity.explanation: Each multiplication adds 2 to the upper-right entry, so after four copies it is \(2\cdot 4=8\). The 16 choice incorrectly powers the entry 2 to the fourth power.

title: Use a nonzero determinant and verify the identity

section.heading: Use a nonzero determinant and verify the identity
body: A \(2\times 2\) matrix with rows(a, b), (c, d)has determinant ad−bc. It has a multiplicative inverse exactly when this is nonzero; the inverse has rows(d, −b), (−c, a), all divided by the determinant. A diagonal matrix therefore inverts its nonzero diagonal entries. Verify by multiplying to obtain diagonal 1 s and off-diagonal 0 s, rather than negating or inverting every entry independently.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For A with rows(2, 3), (1, 2), the determinant is \(4-3=1\). Its inverse has rows(2, −3), (−1, 2). The first product entry is \(2\cdot 2+3 \left(-1\right)=1\) and the next is \(2 \left(-3\right)+3\cdot 2=0\); the second row similarly gives 0, 1. A zero determinant would make division impossible.

activity.prompt: What is the determinant of a matrix with rows(4, 1), (6, 2)?
activity.explanation: Compute \(ad-bc=4\cdot 2-1\cdot 6=2\). The 14 choice adds the two diagonal products; the−2 choice reverses their subtraction order.

title: Distinguish an arithmetic term from its partial sum

section.heading: Distinguish an arithmetic term from its partial sum
body: An arithmetic sequence has constant difference d. With first term \(a_{1}\), the nth term is \(a_{1}+\left(n-1\right) d\), because there are n−1 jumps after the first. The first n terms sum to \(\frac{n \left(a_{1}+a_{n}\right)}{2}\): opposite-end pairs have the same total. A negative difference makes later terms decrease but does not change the indexing or sum formula.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(a_{1}=9\) and \(d=-2\), the eighth term is \(9+7 \left(-2\right)=-5\). The first-eight sum is \(\frac{8 \left(9-5\right)}{2}=16\). An arithmetic sequence whose first and last terms are 3 and 17 over eight terms instead has mean term 10 and total 80 even before its common difference is calculated.

activity.prompt: For \(a_{1}=2\) and \(d=5\), what is the sum of the first six terms?
activity.explanation: The sixth term is \(2+5\cdot 5=27\). The six-term sum is \(\frac{6 \left(2+27\right)}{2}=87\). The 162 choice multiplies every term by the last value; 72 drops one 5-unit jump in the last term.

title: Count multiplicative jumps and distinguish finite sums

section.heading: Count multiplicative jumps and distinguish finite sums
body: A geometric sequence has constant ratio r. With first term \(a_{1}\), \(a_{n}=a_{1} r^{n-1}\), and the first n terms sum to \(\frac{a_{1} \left(1-r^{n}\right)}{1-r}\) for \(r\ne 1\). If \(r=1\), the sum is \(na_{1}\). An infinite sum exists only when \(\lvert r\rvert <1\) and equals \(\frac{a_{1}}{1-r}\). A distant term can determine r from the number of jumps, not from the destination index alone.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For 8, 4, 2, …, ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\) gives fourth term 1, first-four sum 15 and infinite sum 16. If \(a_{1}=3\) and \(a_{4}=81\) with positive ratio, then \(3 r^{3}=81\), so \(r=3\) and \(a_{6}=3\cdot 3^{5}=729\). The first-to-fourth gap contains three multiplications.

activity.prompt: A geometric sequence starts 10, 5, 2.5, … . What is its infinite sum?
activity.explanation: The ratio is \(\frac{1}{2}\) with magnitude below 1, so \(\text{sum}=\frac{10}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=20\). The 15 choice sums just the first two terms; it does not include all later positive terms.

title: Undo a fractional power with its reciprocal exponent

section.heading: Undo a fractional power with its reciprocal exponent
body: For a positive base, \(a^{\frac{m}{n}}\) means the nth root raised to m. Products of equal bases add exponents, quotients subtract them, and powers of powers multiply them. To undo \(x^{p}=A\) for positive x, raise both sides to \(\frac{1}{p}\) when \(p\ne 0\). Express bases such as 4 or 8 as powers of 2 before matching an exponent equation.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(27^{\frac{4}{3}}\), take the cube root 3 then the fourth power 81. If positive x satisfies \(x^{\frac{3}{2}}=64\), raising both sides to \(\frac{2}{3}\) gives \(x=16\); checking \(\left(\sqrt{16}\right)^{3}=64\) confirms it. In \(2^{n}\cdot 8^{2}=2^{11}\), rewrite \(8^{2}=2^{6}\) to get \(n=5\).

activity.prompt: For positive x, \(x^{\frac{3}{2}}=216\). What is x?
activity.explanation: Raise 216 to the \(\frac{2}{3}\) power: its cube root is 6 and \(6^{2}=36\). Check \(\left(\sqrt{36}\right)^{3}=6^{3}=216\). The 6 choice stops after the root step.

title: Extract square factors and keep the principal-root sign

section.heading: Extract square factors and keep the principal-root sign
body: For nonnegative a, b, \(\sqrt{a} \sqrt{b}=\sqrt{ab}\). Extract perfect-square factors before combining like radicals, but do not split a root across addition or subtraction. For real x, \(\sqrt{x^{2}}=\lvert x\rvert\), not always x. Thus an equation \(\sqrt{x^{2}}=c\) with \(c>0\) has both \(x=c\) and \(x=-c\), although the principal-root symbol itself is nonnegative.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: \(\sqrt{98}-\sqrt{50}=7 \sqrt{2}-5 \sqrt{2}=2 \sqrt{2}\). For \(\sqrt{16 x^{2}}\), the simplified result is \(4 \lvert x\rvert\): at \(x=-3\) it equals 12, while 4 x would give−12. If \(\sqrt{x^{2}}=9\), both \(\pm 9\) work, so their sum is zero.

activity.prompt: Which expression equals \(\sqrt{75}-\sqrt{12}\)?
activity.explanation: Extract squares: \(\sqrt{75}=5 \sqrt{3}\) and \(\sqrt{12}=2 \sqrt{3}\). Their difference is \(3 \sqrt{3}\). The \(\sqrt{63}\) choice incorrectly puts subtraction inside a single radical.

title: Separate coefficients from powers of ten

section.heading: Separate coefficients from powers of ten
body: In scientific notation \(a\times 10^{n}\) has \(1\le \lvert a\rvert <10\) and integer n. Multiply or divide the coefficients separately; for equal base 10, add exponents under multiplication and subtract them under division. Normalize the coefficient at the end, adjusting the exponent in the opposite direction. Subtracting a negative denominator exponent increases the resulting exponent.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: \(\frac{8\times 10^{-4}}{2\times 10^{3}}=4\times 10^{-7}\). In \(\left(6\times 10^{5}\right) \left(5\times 10^{-2}\right)\), the first product is \(30\times 10^{3}\), which normalizes to \(3\times 10^{4}\). Shifting the coefficient from 30 to 3 divides it by 10, so the power of ten must increase by one.

activity.prompt: What is \(\frac{9\times 10^{-2}}{3\times 10^{-5}}\)?
activity.explanation: The coefficient is \(\frac{9}{3}=3\) and the exponent is \(-2-\left(-5\right)=3\). Thus the answer is \(3\times 10^{3}\). Adding the exponents gives the wrong−7; reversing their subtraction gives−3.

title: Reduce the remainder again after an operation

section.heading: Reduce the remainder again after an operation
body: If N leaves remainder r when divided by positive d, write \(N=dq+r\) with \(0\le r<d\). Substitute this expression into the requested operation; terms containing d contribute remainder zero. The remaining number may still be at least d, so reduce it again. A remainder is not the same as a quotient or the divisor itself.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(N=9 q+5\), then \(3 N+4=27 q+19=9 \left(3 q+2\right)+1\). The new remainder is 1, not the raw value 19. Equivalently, compute \(3\cdot 5+4=19\) and then reduce 19 modulo 9. This works without knowing the original integer N.

activity.prompt: N leaves remainder 4 when divided by 6. What remainder does 2 N+3 leave when divided by 6?
activity.explanation: Write \(N=6 q+4\). Then \(2 N+3=12 q+11=6 \left(2 q+1\right)+5\), so the remainder is 5. The 11 choice has not been reduced to the required range 0 through 5.

title: Build a common multiple from prime powers

section.heading: Build a common multiple from prime powers
body: Factor positive integers into primes. The greatest common factor takes the smaller exponent of each shared prime, while the least common multiple takes the larger exponent of every prime present. Thus gcd(a, b)·lcm \(\left(a,b\right)=ab\). A common multiple must be divisible by each original integer; a common divisor need not be a multiple of either.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(72=2^{3}\cdot 3^{2}\) and \(90=2\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5\), the GCF is \(2\cdot 3^{2}=18\) and the LCM is \(2^{3}\cdot 3^{2}\cdot 5=360\). Checking \(\frac{360}{72}=5\) and \(\frac{360}{90}=4\) confirms divisibility; \(\frac{72\cdot 90}{18}\) also gives 360. Multiplying the two numbers directly usually gives a common multiple larger than the least one.

activity.prompt: What is the least common multiple of 20 and 30?
activity.explanation: Factor \(20=2^{2}\cdot 5\) and \(30=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\). The LCM uses \(2^{2}\cdot 3\cdot 5=60\). The 10 choice is the GCF; 600 is a common multiple but not the least.

title: Keep absolute values, negative bases, and subtraction distinct

section.heading: Keep absolute values, negative bases, and subtraction distinct
body: Absolute value is nonnegative distance from zero. A negative number raised to an odd integer power stays negative, while an even power is nonnegative. Parentheses matter: \(\left(-a\right)^{2}\) and \(-a^{2}\) are different expressions. Evaluate powers and absolute values before addition or subtraction, and remember that subtracting a negative adds its positive counterpart.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: \(\lvert -6\rvert -\left(-3\right)^{3}=6-\left(-27\right)=33\). In contrast, \(-3^{2}=-9\) because the square applies before the leading minus, while \(\left(-3\right)^{2}=9\). Writing the negative base in parentheses prevents a calculator entry from silently changing the intended grouping.

activity.prompt: What is \(\lvert -4\rvert -\left(-2\right)^{3}\)?
activity.explanation: The absolute value is 4 and the cube is−8. Thus \(4-\left(-8\right)=12\). Treating the odd power as positive or forgetting that subtracting a negative adds changes the result.

title: Convert angle units using a full turn

section.heading: Convert angle units using a full turn
body: A full turn measures \(360^\circ\) or \(2 \pi\) radians, so \(180^\circ\) equals \(\pi\) radians. Multiply degrees by \(\frac{\pi }{180}\) to get radians, and radians by \(\frac{180}{\pi }\) to get degrees. Preserve exact multiples of \(\pi\) when possible. A reference angle such as \(60^\circ\) is not the same as a full angle such as \(240^\circ\), even when their trigonometric magnitudes are related.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(330^\circ\), multiply \(\frac{330 \pi }{180}\) and reduce to \(\frac{11 \pi }{6}\). Reversing the conversion gives \(\left(\frac{11 \pi }{6}\right) \left(\frac{180}{\pi }\right)=330^\circ\). Since \(330^\circ\) is between \(270^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\), the radian measure should lie between \(\frac{3 \pi }{2}\) and \(2 \pi\), which \(\frac{11 \pi }{6}\) does.

activity.prompt: What is \(300^\circ\) in radians?
activity.explanation: Compute \(\frac{300 \pi }{180}=\frac{5 \pi }{3}\). The \(\frac{2 \pi }{3}\) choice describes \(120^\circ\), a different angle, while \(\frac{3 \pi }{5}\) reverses the intended conversion ratio.

title: Rotate coordinate signs in the stated direction

section.heading: Rotate coordinate signs in the stated direction
body: For rotations about the origin, \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise maps(x, y)to(−y, x), \(90^\circ\) clockwise maps it to(y, −x), and \(180^\circ\) maps it to(−x, −y). Counterclockwise follows the usual positive-angle direction. The squared distance \(x^{2}+y^{2}\) must remain unchanged, providing a quick check; a reflection can preserve distance but still turn the wrong way.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Rotating \(\left(3,-5\right) 90^\circ\) counterclockwise gives(5, 3). Both points have squared radius 34. A clockwise turn would give(−5, −3), while changing both signs produces \(a 180^\circ\) turn to(−3, 5). These operations are distinct despite all preserving distance from the origin.

activity.prompt: What is the image of(−4, 7)under \(a 90^\circ\) clockwise turn about the origin?
activity.explanation: The clockwise rule sends(x, y)to(y, −x), giving(7, 4). The point (−7, −4) is the counterclockwise image. The point (4, −7) reverses both signs, a \(180^\circ\) turn.

title: Use prime-exponent parity to prove a square condition

section.heading: Use prime-exponent parity to prove a square condition
body: A positive integer is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorization is even. Multiplying by n adds the prime exponents from n. To make several products squares simultaneously, each prime must impose compatible parity requirements on n; one requirement can demand an even exponent while another demands odd, proving impossibility for every positive integer rather than just tested examples.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(45 n=3^{2}\cdot 5\cdot n\) to be a square, n needs an odd exponent of 5 and even exponents of other unpaired primes; the least choice is \(n=5\), giving 225. But 3 n and 5 n cannot both be squares: the exponent of 3 in n must be odd for 3 n and even for 5 n, a contradiction. A decimal approximation is not a proof.

activity.prompt: What is the least positive integer n for which 28 n is a perfect square?
activity.explanation: Factor \(28=2^{2}\cdot 7\). Only the exponent of 7 is odd, so multiply by 7 to obtain \(196=14^{2}\). Multiplying by 14 would make the exponent of 2 odd instead of fixing all exponents.

title: Split a total into all the ratio parts

section.heading: Split a total into all the ratio parts
body: For a ratio a: b, the complete total contains a+b parts. Divide the total by a+b to find one part, then multiply by the requested number of parts. A fraction of a total uses the same idea: divide by its denominator and multiply by its numerator. A group-to-group ratio \(\frac{a}{b}\) is different from the group’s fraction \(\frac{a}{a+b}\) of the whole.

If only one group size is given, instead divide it by that group’s ratio parts before finding the other group. For a boys: girls ratio 2: 5 with 30 girls, one part is 6 and there are 12 boys; 30 is not the combined total.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: In a4: 7 split of 66 objects, there are 11 parts, each containing 6 objects. The first group has 24 and the second 42. Its fraction of the total is \(\frac{4}{11}\), not \(\frac{4}{7}\). Likewise, five twelfths of 72 is \(\frac{72}{12}\cdot 5=30\).

activity.prompt: Red: blue is 3: 8 and there are 77 beads total. How many are red?
activity.explanation: There are 11 parts, giving \(\frac{77}{11}=7\) per part. Three red parts contain 21 beads. Using \(\frac{3}{8}\) of the total confuses a red-to-blue ratio with a red-to-total fraction; 56 is the blue count.

title: Name the reference amount for a percentage

section.heading: Name the reference amount for a percentage
body: Percent means a fraction of a named base: \(\text{percent}=\frac{\text{part}}{\text{base}}\)\(· 100\). Percent change uses the original amount; margin uses selling price; markup uses cost; percent error uses the specified true value. A commission is its percentage times sales, then add any fixed pay. Identify the denominator in words before calculating so equally meaningful percentages do not get interchanged.

If a known part equals p%of an unknown base, solve \(\frac{p}{100}\cdot\text{base}=\text{part}\), so \(\text{base}=\frac{\text{part}}{p/100}\). Dividing by the percent factor reverses the stated share; it does not mean taking that percentage of the known part again.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: An item costing 60 and selling for 75 has profit 15. Its markup is \(\frac{15}{60}=25\%\), but its margin is \(\frac{15}{75}=20\%\). For a weekly base 180 plus 6%of 2000 sales, total earnings are \(180+120=300\). The commission applies to sales, not to the fixed pay or the combined total.

activity.prompt: A fee rises from 80 to 100. What is the percent increase?
activity.explanation: The increase is 20 and the original base is 80, so \(\frac{20}{80}=25\%\). The 20%choice divides by the new fee 100; 125%is the new amount as a percentage of the original, not the increase.

title: Multiply successive factors and divide to reverse them

section.heading: Multiply successive factors and divide to reverse them
body: A p%increase multiplies the current amount by \(1+\frac{p}{100}\); a decrease multiplies by \(1-\frac{p}{100}\). Successive changes multiply their factors because each uses the amount at that step. Recover an original amount by dividing by the complete retained factor. Equal increases and decreases do not cancel: \(\left(1+r\right) \left(1-r\right)=1-r^{2}\).

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A price 300 raised 10%then reduced 25%becomes \(300\cdot 1.10\cdot 0.75=247.50\). If that final price were given instead, dividing 247.50 by 0.825 recovers 300. To undo a25%increase, an original 100 became 125 and must drop \(\frac{25}{125}=20\%\); the reverse percentage uses the larger base.

activity.prompt: After a20%increase and a10%discount, a price is 216. What was the original?
activity.explanation: The complete factor is \(1.20\cdot 0.90=1.08\). Thus \(\text{original}=\frac{216}{1.08}=200\). Adding the signed percentages as though they share one base gives the wrong inverse.

title: Cancel units and square an area conversion

section.heading: Cancel units and square an area conversion
body: A conversion factor compares equal amounts and therefore equals one. Put the old unit in a denominator so it cancels. For area or volume, square or cube the length factor. Convert rate numerators and denominators separately. For a tile purchase, divide floor area by one tile’s area, multiply by the required extra fraction, round up to whole packs, then multiply by cost per pack.

\(\text{density}=\frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\), so \(\text{mass}=\text{density}\times\text{volume}\). A density \(\frac{20 \text{kg}}{m^{3}}\) and volume \(0.45 m^{3}\) give mass 9 kg as the cubic-meter units cancel. To buy p%extra, multiply the required count by \(1+\frac{p}{100}\), not just \(\frac{p}{100}\); then enforce whole packs.

Distance divided by fuel efficiency(miles per gallon)gives gallons: \(\frac{120\text{ miles}}{30\text{ miles/gallon}}=4\text{ gallons}\). Multiply by price per gallon only after recovering the fuel amount.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: An 8-by-10 meter floor has area \(80 m^{2}\). A square tile of side \(40 \text{cm}=0.4 m\) has area \(0.16 m^{2}\), so 500 tiles cover it. Buying 6%extra needs 530 tiles; packs of 24 require ceil \(\left(\frac{530}{24}\right)=23\) packs. At 14 per pack the minimum cost is 322. Separately, \(\frac{\frac{54 \text{km}}{h}\cdot 1000}{3600}=\frac{15 m}{s}\); both distance and time units change.

activity.prompt: How many square centimeters equal 3 square meters?
activity.explanation: One meter is 100 centimeters, so one square meter is \(100^{2}=10000\) square centimeters. Multiply by 3 to obtain 30000. A one-dimensional factor misses the second direction of area.

title: Conserve the ingredient, not the percentage

section.heading: Conserve the ingredient, not the percentage
body: A weighted concentration or unit cost is \(\frac{\text{total ingredient or cost}}{\text{total amount}}\). Multiply each component’s amount by its concentration or unit value before adding. If an unknown amount is present, set this weighted expression equal to the target and solve; pure water adds volume but zero solute. Group attendance works identically: convert each percentage into an actual attendee count before combining.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Mixing 3 liters at 10%and 7 at 30%gives \(\frac{0.3+2.1}{10}=24\%\). For 9 liters at 30%diluted to 15%, the solute remains 2.7 liters. Final volume must be \(\frac{2.7}{0.15}=18\), so 9 liters of water are added. An unweighted average ignores unequal amounts; final volume is different from added volume.

activity.prompt: Four pounds at 3 per pound are mixed with six pounds at 8 per pound. What is the ingredient cost per pound?
activity.explanation: Total cost is \(4\cdot 3+6\cdot 8=60\) over 10 pounds, giving 6 per pound. The 5.50 choice averages the two prices equally; 60 is total cost instead of unit cost.

title: Divide total distance by total travel time

section.heading: Divide total distance by total travel time
body: Average speed is total distance divided by total time. Compute each leg’s time as \(\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}\), add the times, then divide the combined distance by that total. Averaging the speeds directly is valid for equal amounts of time, not equal distances. Include any stated stops in the total time if the question asks for the overall trip.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A trip covers 90 miles at 45 mph and 60 miles at 60 mph. Its times are 2 and 1 hour, so average speed is \(\frac{150}{3}=50\) mph. The arithmetic mean 52.5 mph incorrectly assigns equal time to both legs. For equal distances, the slower leg takes longer and pulls the average toward the slower speed.

activity.prompt: A driver goes 60 miles at 20 mph and 60 miles at 60 mph. What is the overall average speed?
activity.explanation: The two legs take 3 and 1 hour, so the trip covers 120 miles in 4 hours. Its average is 30 mph. The 40 mph choice is the unweighted mean of the two speeds.

title: Add signed rates after accounting for completed work

section.heading: Add signed rates after accounting for completed work
body: Use amount per unit time, not completion times: a machine finishing one job in a hours has rate \(\frac{1}{a}\). Add simultaneous productive rates and subtract opposing drains. For a delayed helper, compute the first worker’s completed fraction, then divide the remaining fraction by the new combined rate. Identical workers add proportional capacity; preserve the units when the output is parts rather than normalized jobs.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A needs 10 hours and B needs 15 hours alone. If A works alone for 2 hours, it finishes \(\frac{1}{5}\) and leaves \(\frac{4}{5}\). Together their rate is \(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{15}=\frac{1}{6}\) job/hour, so the remaining time is \(\frac{\frac{4}{5}}{\frac{1}{6}}=4.8\) hours. Total elapsed time would be 6.8 hours, a different requested quantity.

activity.prompt: Pump A fills in 8 hours and pump B fills in 24 hours. How long do they take together?
activity.explanation: The combined rate is \(\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{24}=\frac{1}{6}\) tank per hour. Its reciprocal is 6 hours. Averaging or adding the completion times does not represent simultaneous work.

title: Use actual counts when ratios change

section.heading: Use actual counts when ratios change
body: Write original quantities as common-multiplier counts, such as ak, bk. Add or subtract the stated real amounts from those counts, then impose the new ratio with an equation. For linked ratios, make the shared quantity use the same number of parts before comparing the outside quantities. A ratio part is not automatically one year, bead, or person.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If original \(\text{red}:\text{blue}=3:5\), counts are 3 k, 5 k. Adding 8 reds and removing 4 blues to obtain 1: 1 gives \(3 k+8=5 k-4\), so \(k=6\) and the original total 48. For \(a:b=3:4\) and \(b:c=6:7\), scale to 9: 12 and 12: 14, giving \(a:c=9:14\).

activity.prompt: Two ages are currently 1: 3. In 6 years they will be 1: 2. What is the younger age now?
activity.explanation: Write ages k, 3 k. The future ratio requires \(2 \left(k+6\right)=3 k+6\), giving \(k=6\). The current younger age is 6, not the older 18 or the future younger 12.

title: Convert flow units before finding the new fill time

section.heading: Convert flow units before finding the new fill time
body: For a fixed reservoir volume, \(V=\text{rate}\times\text{time}\) and \(\text{new time}=\frac{V}{\text{new rate}}\). Convert minutes and hours before forming either product. A slower pump needs more time for the same volume, so fill time varies inversely with flow rate. This is an integrated unit-and-rate problem: comparing bare numbers with different rate units is invalid.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A reservoir fills in 3 hours at 16 liters per minute. Its volume is \(3\cdot 60\cdot 16=2880\) liters. A replacement pump supplies 720 liters per hour, so it needs \(\frac{2880}{720}=4\) hours. The new pump is slower than the old 960 liters per hour, so the longer time is reasonable.

activity.prompt: A reservoir takes 4 hours to fill at 15 liters per minute. How many hours would a600-liter-per-hour pump need?
activity.explanation: The volume is \(4\cdot 60\cdot 15=3600\) liters. Dividing by 600 liters per hour gives 6 hours. Keeping the old 4 hours ignores the slower pump; 0.1 results from mixing minutes with hours.

title: Track the gap or the full distance that must clear

section.heading: Track the gap or the full distance that must clear
body: For travelers approaching, their separation closes at the sum of their speeds. For same-direction catch-up, use the positive difference, after computing any head start as \(\text{speed}\times\text{delay}\). A train fully crossing a bridge must move its front by train length plus bridge length so the rear clears. \(\text{time}=\frac{\text{required distance}}{\text{relative rate}}\), using one time unit and the correct starting event.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Two travelers 300 miles apart approaching at 60 and 90 mph meet after \(\frac{300}{150}=2\) hours. A 120-meter train crossing a280-meter bridge at \(\frac{25 m}{s}\) requires \(\frac{400}{25}=16\) seconds from front entry to rear exit. Using just the bridge length would stop the clock when the front, not the rear, leaves.

activity.prompt: Two cyclists start 84 miles apart and ride toward each other at 12 and 16 mph. How long until they meet?
activity.explanation: The gap closes at \(12+16=28\) mph. Time is \(\frac{84}{28}=3\) hours. The 21 choice incorrectly uses the difference 4 mph, appropriate to a different same-direction situation.

title: Add the fixed amount once and every repeated payment

section.heading: Add the fixed amount once and every repeated payment
body: A total with a fixed initial amount F and n identical later payments p has total F+np. Multiply the repeated amount by the actual number of payments before adding the initial charge. The word followed by usually means the initial payment is additional, not one of those repeated installments. Check that the final result includes every amount exactly once.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A 45 down payment followed by four 80 payments totals \(45+4\cdot 80=365\). Reporting 320 omits the down payment; multiplying \(\left(45+80\right)\) by 4 would repeat the initial payment four times. A short table labeling initial and repeated charges can prevent both mistakes.

activity.prompt: A purchase has a30 down payment followed by five 40 payments. What is the total?
activity.explanation: Five repeated payments total 200. Add the single 30 down payment to obtain 230. The 200 choice omits it, while 350 repeats the fixed amount with every installment.

title: Separate a starting amount from a per-unit change

section.heading: Separate a starting amount from a per-unit change
body: A linear model has output F+rx, where F is the starting amount and r is change per input unit. From two observations, \(r=\frac{\text{output change}}{\text{input change}}\), then substitute one point to obtain F. Compare two plans by equating or comparing their complete expressions. Average cost is total cost divided by item count. A retained fraction of income followed by a fixed expense is also a linear model.

For price p, per-item cost v and fixed cost F, profit is(p−v)q−F. Break-even solves \(\text{profit}=0\), so \(q=\frac{F}{p-v}\) when \(p>v\). Use the contribution p−v, not the full selling price, to cover fixed cost.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A rental costs 32 for 3 hours and 56 for 7 hours. The hourly rate is \(\frac{24}{4}=6\) and the fixed charge \(32-18=14\), giving \(C \left(h\right)=14+6 h\). For a30 total, \(h=\frac{30-14}{6}=\frac{8}{3}\) hours. If monthly income I retains 75%after savings and then pays 24 transportation, remaining spending is 0.75 I−24, preserving both the percentage and fixed amount.

activity.prompt: A service costs 18 plus 4 per item. Another costs 30 plus 2 per item. At how many items do their costs match?
activity.explanation: Set \(18+4 n=30+2 n\), so \(2 n=12\) and \(n=6\). At six items both cost 42. Dividing the fixed-charge difference by just one rate ignores the other plan’s variable cost.

title: Use count and value equations together

section.heading: Use count and value equations together
body: For two types of objects, define one variable for each count. One equation describes their total number; another multiplies each count by its price or value. Substitute one count as total minus the other, solve, and verify both original equations. A correct individual count can still be the wrong answer if the question asks for the other type.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A show sells 70 tickets: adults cost 11 and students 6, with total revenue 520. If a is adults, \(11 a+6 \left(70-a\right)=520\). Thus \(5 a=100\) and \(a=20\), leaving 50 students. Check \(20+50=70\) and \(220+300=520\). Using the average ticket price alone loses the integer-count relationship.

activity.prompt: Tickets cost 10 for adults and 4 for children. There are 50 tickets totaling 320. How many adult tickets were sold?
activity.explanation: Let a be adults. Then \(10 a+4 \left(50-a\right)=320\), giving \(6 a=120\) and \(a=20\). The other 30 tickets are children, a common requested-quantity trap.

title: Create one variable and check the allowed vertex

section.heading: Create one variable and check the allowed vertex
body: For \(f \left(x\right)=ax^{2}+bx+c\) with \(a<0\), the maximum over all real x occurs at \(x=\frac{-b}{2 a}\); substitute that input to obtain the maximum output. Use a constraint to eliminate another variable before maximizing a rectangle’s area or revenue. For a restricted interval, an outside vertex is unavailable: compare endpoints instead. Keep input quantities, outputs, and physical restrictions distinct.

A rectangle has area xy and full perimeter 2 x+2 y; fencing only three sides changes that constraint. Revenue is price×quantity, so a demand relation must be substituted into that product before locating its maximum.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: With 40 meters fencing three sides of a rectangle, \(2 x+y=40\) and area \(x \left(40-2 x\right)\) peaks at \(x=10\), \(y=20\), area 200. If profit \(P \left(q\right)=-q^{2}+12 q-8\) is limited to \(0\le q\le 4\), its unrestricted vertex 6 is forbidden; the allowed maximum is \(P \left(4\right)=24\). A quadratic with vertex(h, k)and leading coefficient a is \(a \left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\).

activity.prompt: For \(P \left(q\right)=-q^{2}+10 q-9\) with \(0\le q\le 3\), what is its greatest allowed value?
activity.explanation: The unrestricted vertex is \(q=5\), outside the interval. The function is increasing through \(0\le q\le 3\), so use \(q=3:-9+30-9=12\). The 16 choice is the unavailable unrestricted maximum.

title: Choose the physical zero after launch

section.heading: Choose the physical zero after launch
body: Ground contact occurs where height equals zero, not where height is largest. Factor or use the quadratic formula to solve the height equation, then retain times consistent with the model’s physical domain. A zero at \(t=0\) is the launch if the object starts on the ground; a later positive zero is its return. Negative times precede launch and are not future contacts.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(h \left(t\right)=-3 t^{2}+18 t\), factor \(-3 t \left(t-6\right)=0\). The zeros are 0 and 6; the ball returns after 6 seconds. Its peak occurs halfway at \(t=3\) with height 27, so the time 3 answers a different question. If launch height were nonzero, test the roots rather than assuming symmetry around zero.

activity.prompt: For \(h \left(t\right)=-4 t^{2}+28 t\), when does the object first return to the ground after launch?
activity.explanation: Set \(-4 t \left(t-7\right)=0\). The launch is \(t=0\) and the later zero is \(t=7\). The 3.5 choice is the peak time, not the return time.

title: Model lengths before computing perimeter or area

section.heading: Model lengths before computing perimeter or area
body: Name an unknown side x and express related sides in terms of x. A rectangle has perimeter 2(length+width)and area(length)(width). If a side increases, subtract the original area from the new area, retaining cross terms when expanding a square. Solve the resulting equation and reject negative physical dimensions. Check whether the question requests the side, the other side, or the area.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If a rectangle’s sides are x and x+2 and its perimeter is 44, then \(4 x+4=44\) gives \(x=10\) and area 120. If a square’s side increases by 3 and its area increases by 51, then \(\left(x+3\right)^{2}-x^{2}=6 x+9=51\), giving \(x=7\). Canceling the \(x^{2}\) terms does not cancel the cross term 6 x.

activity.prompt: A rectangle has width x, length x+4, and area 45. What is its width?
activity.explanation: The equation \(x \left(x+4\right)=45\) becomes \(\left(x+9\right) \left(x-5\right)=0\). The positive width is 5, giving length 9 and area 45. The 9 choice reports the length, while−9 is not a valid physical dimension.

title: Count periods and compare exponential ratios

section.heading: Count periods and compare exponential ratios
body: Repeated percentage change uses \(P \left(t\right)=P_{0} b^{t}\), with \(b=1+r\) for growth or 1−r for decay; the exponent counts periods. Half-life h uses \(P_{0} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{h}}\). Infer b from ratios across the actual input gap. For comparing two positive exponential models, divide them to isolate a ratio of bases, use logarithms if needed, and check the neighboring whole periods for the first strict threshold.

When a ratio of growth bases is greater than 1, its logarithm is positive. If it is between 0 and 1, dividing an inequality by that negative logarithm reverses its direction. Check the original models at adjacent whole periods to verify any threshold.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A 160-gram sample with half-life 5 days has \(160 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3}=20\) grams after 15 days. For \(A=500 \left(1.3\right)^{t}\) and \(B=900 \left(1.1\right)^{t}\), \(A>B\) means \(\left(\frac{13}{11}\right)^{t}>1.8\), giving \(t>\frac{\ln 1.8}{\ln \left(\frac{13}{11}\right)}\approx 3.52\). The first whole period is 4; at 3, \(A=1098.5<B=1197.9\), while at 4, \(A\approx 1428.05>B\approx 1317.69\).

activity.prompt: A quantity starts at 500 and loses 10%per year. What does the model predict after 2 years?
activity.explanation: Each year retains 90%, so \(500 \left(0.9\right)^{2}=405\). Subtracting 50 twice gives 400 but models a fixed loss; 450 is only one year of decay.

title: Separate simple interest from compounding periods

section.heading: Separate simple interest from compounding periods
body: With principal P, annual decimal rate r, and years t, simple interest gives balance P(1+rt): interest is based on the original principal. Compounding n times per year gives \(P\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\), because each period earns interest on the current balance. Use matching rate and period units, and add principal if the question asks for final balance rather than interest earned.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: At 800 principal and 5%annual simple interest for 3 years, interest is 120 and balance 920. Compounding semiannually for the same time instead uses \(800 \left(1.025\right)^{6}\). The exponent 6 counts two periods in each of three years; using 5%every half-year would double the stated annual rate.

activity.prompt: What expression gives 600 at 8%annual interest compounded quarterly for 3 years?
activity.explanation: The quarterly rate is \(\frac{0.08}{4}=0.02\) and there are \(4\cdot 3=12\) quarters, giving \(600 \left(1.02\right)^{12}\). The other expressions mismatch the annual rate or the number of periods.

title: Charge each rate only to its own part

section.heading: Charge each rate only to its own part
body: A tiered cost rule changes at a threshold. Separate the included units from additional units and apply each rate only to its portion. A base fee that already covers the first u units gives F+r(x−u)for \(x>u\), not F+rx. A rule applying a price to each of the first n items instead charges that first group n·price before adding the remaining group.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Shipping is 6 for up to 4 kilograms and 2 per kilogram beyond 4. A 7-kilogram parcel costs \(6+2 \left(7-4\right)=12\). If the first 8 tickets cost 9 each and additional tickets 5 each, 11 tickets cost \(8\cdot 9+3\cdot 5=87\). Giving all tickets the lower additional rate would discard the first tier.

activity.prompt: Using the shipping rule 6 for up to 4 kg plus 2 per kilogram beyond 4, what is the cost for 9 kg?
activity.explanation: Only \(9-4=5\) kilograms receive the additional rate. Cost is \(6+2\cdot 5=16\). The 24 choice charges every kilogram again; 10 omits the covered base fee.

title: Round in the direction required by the inequality

section.heading: Round in the direction required by the inequality
body: Solve the model before enforcing whole numbers. To reach a minimum, round a noninteger lower bound upward; for a maximum affordable count, round an upper bound downward. A strict inequality excludes equality, so an integer threshold may need the next whole number. Required containers use \(\left\lceil\frac{\text{items}}{\text{capacity}}\right\rceil\), even if the last container is partly empty. Preserve any starting balance or fixed charge.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A balance 40 plus 18 per week reaches at least 150 when \(w\ge \frac{110}{18}\), so first whole week 7 works. A budget 200 with fixed 70 plus 18 per item allows \(n\le \frac{130}{18}\), giving at most 7 items. If one plan becomes cheaper only for \(n>5\), the first whole count is 6, not 5.

activity.prompt: A balance starts at 30 and gains 8 after each week. What is the first whole week with at least 80?
activity.explanation: Solve \(30+8 w\ge 80\), so \(w\ge 6.25\). Round upward to 7. At 6 weeks the balance is 78, still too small; ignoring the starting 30 would use the wrong threshold.

title: Find the best whole-number combination

section.heading: Find the best whole-number combination
body: Use whole counts: 0, 1, 2, and so on. A proposed pair must stay within every resource limit.
To prove a maximum, first find a value no allowed pair can beat. Multiply each limit by zero or a positive number, then add. Choose multipliers that make the left side equal the profit formula.
Find the multipliers by matching the numbers in front of x and y. This gives two equations. Negative multipliers cannot safely keep an upper bound.
If profit must be a whole number, round a fractional upper bound down. Then find an allowed pair that reaches it. A bound alone does not prove the best pair exists.
If only a nonwhole intersection reaches a whole bound M, no whole pair reaches M. Try M−1 and check an actual pair; do not just round each coordinate.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Find the largest \(3x+2y\) for whole counts \(x,y\ge0\), with \(2x+y\le13\) and \(x+2y\le13\). Choose multipliers u and v to match the profit: \(2u+v=3\) and \(u+2v=2\). Double the second equation and subtract the first: \(3v=1\), so \(v=\frac13\) and \(u=\frac43\). Multiply the first limit by \(\frac43\) and the second by \(\frac13\), then add: profit is at most \(\frac{65}{3}=21\frac23\). Since profit is whole, it is at most 21. Try \(x=5,y=3\): the limits give 13 and 11, both allowed, and profit is 21. An allowed pair reaches the upper bound, so 21 is the maximum.

activity.prompt: Whole-number x, \(y\ge 0\) satisfy \(x+y\le 8\) and \(2 x+y\le 12\). What is the maximum 3 x+2 y?
activity.explanation: Adding the two constraints gives \(3 x+2 y\le 20\). The pair(4, 4)satisfies both and attains 20, so this is a proven maximum. The 24 choice violates a resource limit.

title: Use observed minus predicted to evaluate a model

section.heading: Use observed minus predicted to evaluate a model
body: A residual is observed output minus the model’s predicted output at the same input. Positive means the observation is above the prediction; negative means the model overpredicted. Evaluate each input separately before adding residuals. A repeating curved pattern in residuals can reveal a model mismatch, while matching a few points does not justify unrestricted extrapolation.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For prediction \(\hat y=1+3 x\), observations at \(x=1\), 2, 3 are 5, 6, 11. Predictions are 4, 7, 10, so residuals are 1, −1, 1 and their sum 1. Reversing the subtraction would reverse every sign. Each residual belongs to its own input, not to the average of all observations.

activity.prompt: For \(\hat y=3+2 x\), observed outputs at \(x=1\) and 2 are 6 and 5. What is the residual sum?
activity.explanation: The predictions are 5 and 7. Residuals are \(6-5=1\) and \(5-7=-2\), whose sum is−1. Using predicted minus observed would give+1.

title: Recover the slope and intercept before extrapolating

section.heading: Recover the slope and intercept before extrapolating
body: A linear function has the form \(f \left(x\right)=mx+b\). From two input-output pairs, compute \(m=\frac{\text{output change}}{\text{input change}}\), then substitute either pair to find b. If f(0)is given, it is already the intercept. Extending a line uses the same additive rate per input unit, not a constant output ratio unless the intercept is zero.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If \(f \left(2\right)=9\) and \(f \left(6\right)=21\), the slope is \(\frac{21-9}{6-2}=3\). Substituting \(9=3\cdot 2+b\) gives \(b=3\), so \(f \left(10\right)=33\). Dividing 21 by 9 would compare outputs but does not recover the slope because the original line has a nonzero intercept.

activity.prompt: A linear function has \(f \left(0\right)=-2\) and \(f \left(3\right)=7\). What is f(5)?
activity.explanation: The slope is \(\frac{7-\left(-2\right)}{3}=3\) and the intercept is−2, so \(f \left(5\right)=3\cdot 5-2=13\). The 15 choice omits the intercept.

title: Complete the square or evaluate the vertex input

section.heading: Complete the square or evaluate the vertex input
body: For \(f \left(x\right)=ax^{2}+bx+c\) with \(a\ne 0\), the vertex input is \(h=\frac{-b}{2 a}\) and its output is \(k=f \left(h\right)\). Rewriting as \(a \left(x-h\right)^{2}+k\) gives the same point. A positive a leaves a minimum; a negative a gives a maximum. The coefficient b, the minimizing input h, and the minimum output k are different quantities.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(3 x^{2}-12 x+8\), \(h=\frac{12}{6}=2\) and \(k=12-24+8=-4\). Completing the square gives \(3 \left(x-2\right)^{2}-4\), confirming vertex(2, −4). The square term vanishes at the vertex, making the minimum output−4 rather than the input 2.

activity.prompt: What is the vertex of \(f \left(x\right)=x^{2}-8 x+13\)?
activity.explanation: The input is \(h=\frac{8}{2}=4\). Evaluating gives \(16-32+13=-3\), so the vertex is(4, −3). Equivalently, \(f \left(x\right)=\left(x-4\right)^{2}-3\).

title: Identify the hypotenuse before finding a missing side

section.heading: Identify the hypotenuse before finding a missing side
body: In a right triangle the hypotenuse c faces the right angle and satisfies \(a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}\). If the hypotenuse is known, subtract the known leg’s square before taking the positive root. A rectangle’s diagonal is its right-triangle hypotenuse. Recognize scaled triples 3–4–5, 5–12–13, and 8–15–17, but verify which side is largest before using a remembered pattern.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A rectangle has diagonal 25 and one side 7. The other side is \(\sqrt{25^{2}-7^{2}}=\sqrt{576}=24\), so its area is \(7\cdot 24=168\). Adding \(25^{2}+7^{2}\) would incorrectly treat the diagonal as a leg; multiplying 7 by 25 uses a diagonal in place of a rectangle side.

activity.prompt: A right triangle has hypotenuse 17 and one leg 15. What is the other leg?
activity.explanation: Use \(\sqrt{17^{2}-15^{2}}=\sqrt{64}=8\). The \(\sqrt{514}\) choice adds the squares instead of subtracting a known leg from the hypotenuse square.

title: Use the four-step cycle for integer powers of i

section.heading: Use the four-step cycle for integer powers of i
body: Because \(i^{2}=-1\), the powers repeat in a four-step cycle: \(i^{0}=1\), \(i^{1}=i\), \(i^{2}=-1\), \(i^{3}=-i\), and \(i^{4}=1\). For a nonnegative integer exponent, divide by 4 and use its remainder 0, 1, 2, or 3 to choose the cycle position. Even versus odd alone is insufficient because even powers can equal 1 or−1.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: The exponent 2037 equals \(4\cdot 509+1\), so \(i^{2037}=i\). The exponent 2040 has remainder 0 and gives 1. For \(i^{41}+i^{42}\), the two remainders 1 and 2 give i−1. Reduce each exponent separately before adding complex values.

activity.prompt: What is \(i^{99}\)?
activity.explanation: The exponent 99 leaves remainder 3 upon division by 4, so \(i^{99}=i^{3}=-i\). Taking only oddness would not distinguish the i and−i cycle positions.

title: Compare leading degrees for long-run output

section.heading: Compare leading degrees for long-run output
body: For a rational function whose numerator and denominator have the same degree, the horizontal asymptote is \(y=\frac{\text{numerator leading coefficient}}{\text{denominator leading coefficient}}\). A lower-degree numerator gives \(y=0\). A higher-degree numerator has no horizontal asymptote, though another asymptote may exist. This describes outputs at large \(\lvert x\rvert\) and is different from a vertical denominator-zero line.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(f \left(x\right)=\frac{5 x-3}{2 x+7}\), divide top and bottom by \(x:f \left(x\right)=\frac{5-\frac{3}{x}}{2+\frac{7}{x}}\), which approaches \(\frac{5}{2}\) as \(\lvert x\rvert\) grows. The horizontal asymptote is \(y=\frac{5}{2}\). The denominator zero \(x=\frac{-7}{2}\) is a different, vertical feature.

activity.prompt: What is the horizontal asymptote of \(f \left(x\right)=\frac{4 x+1}{x-6}\)?
activity.explanation: The degrees match, so the leading-coefficient ratio gives \(y=4\). The \(x=6\) choice is the vertical asymptote, and \(y=0\) would apply to a numerator of lower degree.

title: Translate a matrix equation into row equations

section.heading: Translate a matrix equation into row equations
body: In A times the column(x, y)equaling a known column, each row of A produces one linear equation. Multiply a row by the unknown column as a dot product, then solve the resulting system by substitution or elimination. Recover both unknowns and check the complete original product; matching one row alone is insufficient.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If A has rows(2, 1), (1, −1)and \(A \left(x,y\right)^{T}=\left(11,1\right)^{T}\), the equations are \(2 x+y=11\) and \(x-y=1\). Adding yields \(3 x=12\), so \(x=4\) and \(y=3\). The original row outputs are \(8+3=11\) and \(4-3=1\), confirming both equations.

activity.prompt: A has rows(1, 2), (2, 1), and \(A \left(x,y\right)^{T}=\left(8,7\right)^{T}\). What is y?
activity.explanation: The rows give \(x+2 y=8\) and \(2 x+y=7\). Substituting \(x=8-2 y\) into the second gives \(16-3 y=7\), so \(y=3\) and \(x=2\). The 2 choice reports the other unknown.

title: Add matching entries and scale every entry

section.heading: Add matching entries and scale every entry
body: Matrix addition and subtraction require exactly the same dimensions. Combine entries in the same row and column. Scalar multiplication multiplies every entry, including negative entries and zeros. These operations differ from row-by-column matrix multiplication; a scalar multiple cannot change a matrix’s dimensions.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Let A have rows(1, −2), (3, 0)and B have rows(4, 1), (−1, 5). The matrix 2 A+B has rows(6, −3), (5, 5), because each entry is twice its A entry plus the matching B entry. For example, the lower-left entry is \(2\cdot 3+\left(-1\right)=5\).

activity.prompt: A has rows(2, −1), (0, 3). What is the top-right entry of 3 A?
activity.explanation: The scalar 3 multiplies the top-right entry−1 to give−3. Leaving the entry unchanged or adding 3 would perform a different operation.

title: Use definitions rather than decimal guesses

section.heading: Use definitions rather than decimal guesses
body: A rational number is a ratio \(\frac{p}{q}\) of integers with \(q\ne 0\); its decimal terminates or repeats. Irrational numbers cannot be written that way. Rational plus irrational is irrational, and a nonzero rational times irrational is irrational. Two irrationals can sum or multiply to a rational, such as \(\sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}=0\) and \(\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}=2\). The square root of a positive integer is rational exactly when that integer is a perfect square.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: \(\sqrt{49}=7\) is rational, while \(\sqrt{50}=5 \sqrt{2}\) is irrational. The number \(3+\sqrt{2}\) must be irrational: if it were rational, subtracting rational 3 would make \(\sqrt{2}\) rational, a contradiction. By contrast, \(\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{8}=\sqrt{16}=4\) is rational, so the label of each factor alone does not determine the product.

activity.prompt: Which number must be irrational?
activity.explanation: \(\sqrt{81}=9\) and \(\sqrt{5}\cdot \sqrt{5}=5\) are rational. Adding rational 2 to irrational \(\sqrt{3}\) remains irrational; subtracting 2 would otherwise express \(\sqrt{3}\) as a rational difference.

title: Represent even and odd integers algebraically

section.heading: Represent even and odd integers algebraically
body: An even integer is 2 k and an odd integer is 2 k+1 for integer k. Even+even and odd+odd are even; even+odd is odd. A product is even if at least one factor is even and odd only when every factor is odd. Consecutive integers always include an even one, so n(n+1)is even for every integer n. Test claims with these representations rather than a few examples alone.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For odd \(a=2 u+1\) and odd \(b=2 v+1\), their sum is 2(u+v+1), which is even. Their product is 2(2 uv+u+v)+1, which is odd. Also \(n^{2}+n=n \left(n+1\right)\) is always even because one consecutive factor is divisible by 2.
