activity.prompt: For every integer n, which expression is always even?
activity.explanation: The expression \(n^{2}+n\) factors as n(n+1), and one of consecutive integers is even. At \(n=0\), \(n^2+1=1\), so that expression is not always even. The expression \(2n+1\) is always odd.

title: Mirror across an axis or a parallel line

section.heading: Mirror across an axis or a parallel line
body: Reflection across the x-axis maps(x, y)to(x, −y); across the y-axis it maps to(−x, y); across \(y=x\) it swaps to(y, x). Across a vertical line \(x=h\), the horizontal image is 2 h−x; across a horizontal line \(y=k\), the vertical image is 2 k−y. The mirror line is halfway between a point and its image, not necessarily a coordinate axis.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Reflect(8, −3)across \(x=2\) to obtain \(\left(2\cdot 2-8,-3\right)=\left(-4,-3\right)\). The two x-coordinates 8 and−4 average to 2, confirming the mirror. Across \(y=x\), the original point would instead become(−3, 8), a different reflection.

activity.prompt: What is the reflection of(−2, 5)across \(y=1\)?
activity.explanation: The x-coordinate is unchanged and the new y is \(2\cdot 1-5=-3\). The−5 choice reflects across the x-axis rather than the specified line \(y=1\).

title: Scale displacement from the dilation center

section.heading: Scale displacement from the dilation center
body: A dilation with center(h, k)and scale factor s maps(x, y)to(h+s(x−h), k+s(y−k)). Subtract the center, scale the displacement, then add the center back. Corresponding lengths multiply by \(\lvert s\rvert\), areas by \(s^{2}\), and volumes by \(\lvert s\rvert ^{3}\). A dilation about a nonzero center is not the same as multiplying the original coordinates directly.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Dilate \(P=\left(5,1\right)\) by factor 3 about \(C=\left(1,-2\right)\). Its displacement is(4, 3), which scales to(12, 9); the image is(13, 7). The center itself stays fixed. A corresponding triangle’s area would multiply by 9 rather than by 3.

activity.prompt: What is the image of(4, 3)under a factor 2 dilation centered at(1, 1)?
activity.explanation: The displacement from the center is(3, 2). Double to(6, 4), then add(1, 1)to get(7, 5). The 8, 6 choice scales around the origin; 6, 4 forgets to add the center back.

title: Combine parallel-line and triangle angle relationships

section.heading: Combine parallel-line and triangle angle relationships
body: Parallel lines cut by a transversal have equal corresponding and alternate-interior angles, and same-side interior angles sum to \(180^\circ\). Vertical angles are equal at an intersection. A triangle’s angles sum to \(180^\circ\); an isosceles triangle’s equal sides face equal angles. Translate each relationship into an equation and identify which line or triangle supplies it before adding or subtracting angles.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: If one of two same-side interior angles between parallel lines is \(112^\circ\), the other is \(68^\circ\). An isosceles triangle with vertex angle \(44^\circ\) has two equal base angles x, so \(2 x+44=180\) and \(x=68^\circ\). The equality and supplementary relationships are different even when these examples produce the same value.

activity.prompt: An isosceles triangle has vertex angle \(50^\circ\). What is either base angle?
activity.explanation: The two base angles are equal and sum to \(180-50=130^\circ\). Each is \(65^\circ\). The \(130^\circ\) choice is their combined value rather than one angle.

title: Distinguish equal shape from equal size

section.heading: Distinguish equal shape from equal size
body: Congruent triangles have corresponding sides and angles equal; similar triangles may differ by a scale factor. SSS, SAS, and ASA/AAS determine congruence; for right triangles, hypotenuse-leg also works. AAA establishes similarity only. SSA can be ambiguous unless extra information fixes the triangle. Match the included angle in SAS rather than assuming any known angle is sufficient.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: Two triangles each having side lengths 5, 7, 9 are congruent by SSS, even if one is rotated or reflected. Two triangles each with angles \(40^\circ\), \(60^\circ\), \(80^\circ\) need only be similar; one can be twice as large. Two sides and a nonincluded angle do not automatically resolve the sine-law ambiguous case.

activity.prompt: Which information guarantees two triangles are congruent?
choices: One equal side and one equal angle
activity.explanation: SSS fixes the size and shape of a triangle, so matching all three sides guarantees congruence. Matching only angles permits scaling; one side and one angle leave additional freedom.

title: Read the center and semiaxes of an ellipse

section.heading: Read the center and semiaxes of an ellipse
body: An axis-aligned ellipse has \(\frac{\left(x-h\right)^{2}}{A}+\frac{\left(y-k\right)^{2}}{B}=1\) with A, \(B>0\). Its center is(h, k), horizontal semiaxis \(\sqrt{A}\), and vertical semiaxis \(\sqrt{B}\). The major axis follows the larger denominator and has twice that semiaxis length. If \(a\ge b\) denote the major and minor semiaxes, the foci are distance \(c=\sqrt{a^{2}-b^{2}}\) from the center along the major axis.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\frac{\left(x-2\right)^{2}}{36}+\frac{\left(y+1\right)^{2}}{16}=1\), the center is(2, −1), horizontal semiaxis 6 and vertical semiaxis 4. The major-axis length is 12 and its foci are \(\left(2\pm \sqrt{20},-1\right)\). The denominators are squared semiaxis lengths, not the full axis lengths.

activity.prompt: What is the major-axis length of \(\frac{x^{2}}{25}+\frac{y^{2}}{9}=1\)?
activity.explanation: The larger denominator 25 gives semimajor axis 5. The complete major axis extends 5 units on each side of the center, so its length is 10.

title: Use the positive squared term to find the opening direction

section.heading: Use the positive squared term to find the opening direction
body: A horizontal hyperbola has \(\frac{\left(x-h\right)^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{\left(y-k\right)^{2}}{b^{2}}=1\), center(h, k), vertices \(\left(h\pm a,k\right)\), and asymptotes \(y-k=\pm \left(\frac{b}{a}\right) \left(x-h\right)\). If the y term is positive instead, it opens vertically, with vertices \(\left(h,k\pm a\right)\) and slopes \(\frac{\pm a}{b}\) when the positive y denominator is \(a^{2}\). The minus sign distinguishes a hyperbola from an ellipse; focal distance satisfies \(c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}\).

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: For \(\frac{\left(x-1\right)^{2}}{9}-\frac{\left(y+2\right)^{2}}{16}=1\), the center is(1, −2)and vertices are(−2, −2), (4, −2). Its asymptotes are \(y+2=\pm \left(\frac{4}{3}\right) \left(x-1\right)\). The larger denominator 16 does not make it open vertically; the positive x term determines the direction.

activity.prompt: Where are the vertices of \(\frac{x^{2}}{16}-\frac{y^{2}}{9}=1\)?
activity.explanation: The positive x term makes the hyperbola horizontal. Its \(a^{2}=16\) gives \(a=4\), so vertices are 4 units left and right of the origin.

title: Relate a parabola’s focal parameter to its opening

section.heading: Relate a parabola’s focal parameter to its opening
body: For \(\left(x-h\right)^{2}=4 p \left(y-k\right)\), the vertex is(h, k), focus(h, k+p), and directrix \(y=k-p\). Positive p opens upward and negative p opens downward. For \(\left(y-k\right)^{2}=4 p \left(x-h\right)\), the parabola opens horizontally, with focus(h+p, k)and directrix \(x=h-p\). Read p from the coefficient 4 p, not directly from that coefficient.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: In \(\left(y+1\right)^{2}=12 \left(x-2\right)\), the vertex is(2, −1)and \(4 p=12\) gives \(p=3\). It opens right, with focus(5, −1)and directrix \(x=-1\). The point(14, −1)would incorrectly treat 12 as the focal distance rather than four times that distance.

activity.prompt: What is the focus of \(x^{2}=8 y\)?
activity.explanation: Here \(4 p=8\), so \(p=2\) and the parabola opens upward from vertex(0, 0). The focus is(0, 2). Using 8 directly or choosing a horizontal coordinate reads the equation incorrectly.

title: Require one output for each allowed input

section.heading: Require one output for each allowed input
body: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Different inputs may share an output. A relation fails the function test when one allowed input has two different outputs; repeated identical pairs do not create a second output. For a graph, this is the vertical-line test: one vertical line must not hit two different points of the graph.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: The pairs(0, 3), (1, 5), (2, 5)define a function: the shared output 5 is allowed because it belongs to different inputs. The pairs(0, 3), (0, 4), (2, 5)do not define a function, because input 0 would require two different outputs. The direction input→output matters.

activity.prompt: Which relation is a function of x?
activity.explanation: The relation(1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2)gives each input one output; equal outputs for different inputs are allowed. The other relations repeat input 1 or0 with two different outputs.

title: Use an apothem as the perpendicular height

section.heading: Use an apothem as the perpendicular height
body: A regular polygon divides into congruent triangles when the center is joined to every vertex. Each triangle has its polygon side as a base and the apothem as perpendicular height. Adding the triangle areas gives \(A=\frac{\text{perimeter}\times\text{apothem}}{2}\). The apothem is not generally the side or the circumradius; use only the length explicitly perpendicular to a side.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.text: A regular square with side 8 has perimeter 32 and apothem 4. Its area is \(\frac{32\cdot 4}{2}=64\). Four center-to-side triangles each have base 8 and perpendicular height 4, so each contributes 16 and their sum 64 agrees with the square area \(8^{2}\). The apothem is perpendicular to a side, not a slanted center-to-vertex segment.

activity.prompt: A regular hexagon has perimeter 36 and apothem \(3 \sqrt{3}\). What is its area?
activity.explanation: The area is \(\frac{36\cdot 3 \sqrt{3}}{2}=54 \sqrt{3}\). Doubling it omits the half factor; \(18 \sqrt{3}\) would use only part of the given perimeter.
